title: Milestone 3 Overview
text:
Milestone 3 Student Study Guides 
 Transfer Learning & Stronger Segmentation Models (4 November 2026) 
 Welcome to Milestone 3 of the Industrial Surface Anomaly Segmentation curriculum! 
 In  Milestone 1 , you inspected the physical and statistical characteristics of industrial line-scan sensors: unraveling 1-indexed Fortran-order Run-Length Encodings (RLE), analyzing extreme anomaly sparsity across steel strips, and examining the metric penalties imposed by empty, defect-free material. 
 In  Milestone 2 , you constructed your end-to-end baseline systems: establishing clean PyTorch  Dataset  contracts, implementing industrial geometric and photometric augmentations, setting up combination-stratified cross-validation splits, logging experiments to Weights & Biases, training a baseline from-scratch U-Net, and calibrating post-processing decision pipelines. 
 In  Milestone 3 , you elevate your modeling capability from simple baseline networks to state-of-the-art transfer learning architectures:  adapting pretrained vision backbones to single-channel industrial strips, contrasting independent multi-label sigmoid heads against mutually exclusive multi-class softmax partitions, mastering compound loss formulations (BCE + Soft Dice), and conducting rigorous, controlled ablation experiments . 
 
 1. Prerequisites from Milestones 1 and 2 
 Before beginning Milestone 3, ensure you are comfortable with these core concepts established in earlier milestones: 
 
 Industrial Aspect Ratio Awareness : Line-scan sensor images are  \(128 \times 800\)  pixels (anisotropic  \(6.25:1\)  ratio). You understand why square resizing ( \(256 \times 256\) ) distorts thin longitudinal defects and why native resolutions must be preserved. 
 PyTorch Tensor Contracts : You understand the standard segmentation tensor conventions: image inputs of shape  [B, 1, 128, 800]  and multi-label target masks of shape  [B, 4, 128, 800] . 
 Combination Stratification & Leakage Isolation : You know how to group rare defect occurrences into multi-label combination signatures to guarantee stable representation across validation folds without data leakage. 
 The Decision Pipeline : You understand how raw continuous logits map to thresholded binary masks ( \(\tau\) ) and how connected-component minimum area filtering ( \(A_{\min}\) ) suppresses high-frequency sensor noise. 
 RLE Submission Format : You know how to encode binary masks into 1-indexed column-major Fortran strings with the mandatory single-space sentinel ( " " ) for empty predictions. 
 
 
 2. Curriculum Map: Milestone 3 Topics & Study Guides 
 The Milestone 3 curriculum is organized into six focused, progressive learning modules: 
 
 
 
 Milestone 3 Core Topic 
 Primary Study Guide 
 Theoretical Principles 
 Practical Implementation Focus 
 
 
 
 
 1. Encoder–Decoder Architectures 
 Guide 01: Encoder–Decoder Architectures 
 Contracting path, bottleneck, expanding path, receptive fields, skip connections (concatenation vs. addition), spatial dimension alignment on  \(128 \times 800\) . 
 Trace feature tensor shapes through progressive downsampling stages; diagnose spatial phase distortion bugs. 
 
 
 2. Pretrained Backbones 
 Guide 02: Pretrained Backbones & Transfer Learning 
 ImageNet visual feature hierarchies, ResNet residual highways vs. EfficientNet compound MBConv scaling, multi-scale feature taps, freezing vs. fine-tuning, BatchNorm drift. 
 Extract multi-scale feature hierarchies from standard backbones; configure decoders to consume heterogeneous stage channels. 
 
 
 3. Grayscale Input Adaptation 
 Guide 03: Grayscale Input Adaptation 
 Single-channel sensor physics, 3-channel RGB impedance mismatch, 3x channel repeat, first-layer conv weight collapse (sum vs. average), learned  \(1\times 1\)  adapter. 
 Implement and numerically verify activation equivalence across the 3 grayscale adaptation strategies on CPU. 
 
 
 4. Output Heads & Target Semantics 
 Guide 04: Output Heads & Target Semantics 
 4-channel independent Sigmoid vs. 5-channel mutually exclusive Softmax, target representations, mathematical activations, empirical mask overlap audit ( \(\sum m_i \cdot m_j\) ). 
 Audit ground truth masks for pixel-level overlap before choosing a target format; resolve test-time multi-channel collisions. 
 
 
 5. Loss Formulations 
 Guide 05: BCE, Dice, & Compound Losses 
 Extreme class imbalance, numerically stable BCE with logits, differentiable Soft Dice loss, smoothing factor  \(\epsilon\) , compound  \(\text{BCE} + \lambda \text{Dice}\) , loss vs. metric separation. 
 Compare BCE and Soft Dice responses on tiny  \(4\times 4\)  synthetic masks under missed defects, false alarms, and clean sheets. 
 
 
 6. Controlled Experimentation 
 Guide 06: Systematic Model Exploration 
 Scientific single-variable ablation, head and loss compatibility matrix, training trajectory triage (overfitting, erosion, collapse), debugging protocols. 
 Design and execute a 3-phase controlled exploration matrix holding splits, budgets, and post-processing strictly constant. 
 
 
 
 
 3. Guide Overviews & Learning Sequence 
 Follow this recommended reading and implementation sequence: 
 
 
 Guide 01: Encoder–Decoder Architectures for Industrial Segmentation :
  Explains why standard classification features cannot output pixel-aligned masks. Traces a fictional  \(128 \times 800\)  strip through a 4-stage contracting path, bottleneck, and expanding path. Dissects skip connections (concatenation vs. addition), receptive field expansion, and why odd dimensions cause fatal shape errors. 
 
 
 Guide 02: Pretrained Backbones & Transfer Learning: ResNet to EfficientNet :
  Explores what pretrained backbones learn on ImageNet and why low-level edge filters transfer seamlessly to industrial anomaly detection. Compares the architectural building blocks of ResNet (residual shortcuts) and EfficientNet (MBConv, depthwise convolutions, SE attention), and details fine-tuning dynamics and BatchNorm stability. 
 
 
 Guide 03: Adapting Pretrained RGB Backbones to Single-Channel Grayscale :
  Tackles the single-channel sensor dilemma. Works through three defensible adaptation strategies: 3-channel repetition, first-layer convolution weight collapse (sum vs. average), and learned  \(1\times 1\)  adapters. Proves exact numerical activation equivalence and analyzes normalization physics. 
 
 
 Guide 04: Output Heads & Target Semantics: Multi-Label Sigmoid vs. Multi-Class Softmax :
  Contrasts 4-channel independent sigmoid multilabel detection with 5-channel mutually exclusive softmax partitions. Works through a concrete numerical demonstration of a competing-defect pixel, details the step-by-step empirical mask overlap audit, and analyzes permanent information loss when forcing overlapping annotations into integers. 
 
 
 Guide 05: Segmentation Loss Functions: BCE, Dice, & Compound Objectives :
  Addresses extreme class imbalance where  \(97\%+\)  of pixels are clean background. Explains  BCEWithLogitsLoss , derives the differentiable Soft Dice loss with smoothing  \(\epsilon\) , shows how each loss behaves on small missed defects and false alarm speckles, and separates continuous training loss from discrete evaluation metrics. 
 
 
 Guide 06: Systematic Model Exploration & Controlled Experimentation :
  Establishes the single-variable ablation protocol to avoid "alchemy" in deep learning. Details the Milestone 3 Exploration Matrix (Backbone  \(\to\)  Adaptation  \(\to\)  Head/Loss), maps compatible head-loss pairings, and provides a diagnostic guide to triage training failure modes from learning curves. 
 
 
 
 4. Standalone Code Examples & Synthetic Walkthrough 
 To support hands-on learning without disclosing competition training results, this curriculum includes complete, self-contained educational resources built entirely on  synthetic data : 
 1. Interactive Walkthrough Notebook 
 
 Jupyter Notebook :  notebooks/synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Paired Python Script :  notebooks/synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.py 
 Notebook Setup Guide :  notebooks/README.md 
 
 This walkthrough runs on CPU in under 3 seconds and demonstrates feature extraction, grayscale adaptation equivalence, sigmoid vs. softmax probabilities, and compound loss calculation on synthetic  \(128 \times 800\)  strips. 
 2. Standalone Diagnostic Scripts 
 
 
 Feature Map Shape Tracing :  examples/toy_feature_extractor.py 
  Validates contracting path, bottleneck, expanding path, and skip connection tensor dimensions on CPU. 
 
 
 Grayscale Adaptation Equivalence :  examples/toy_grayscale_adaptation.py 
  Numerically proves that first-layer weight summing produces exact mathematical parity with 3-channel input repetition. 
 
 
 Output Head Semantics & Competing Logits :  examples/toy_head_comparison.py 
  Calculates independent Sigmoid vs. mutually exclusive Softmax probabilities and decision outcomes on synthetic competing logits. 
 
 
 BCE vs. Soft Dice Loss Behavior :  examples/toy_loss_behavior.py 
  Evaluates BCE and Soft Dice responses on tiny  \(4\times 4\)  synthetic masks under missed defects, false alarms, and clean empty sheets. 
 
 
 
 5. Teaching Philosophy and Boundaries 
 These study guides are designed as a  guiding hand, not a shortcut : 
 
 They explain the underlying mathematics, tensor dimensions, software interfaces, failure modes, and debugging techniques. 
 They do  not  provide a copy-paste competition training script, pre-computed hyperparameter values, or trained model checkpoints. 
 They do  not  reveal confidential exploratory data analysis findings or performance benchmarks from the private training set. 
 You must write, audit, and debug your own segmentation pipeline against  data/public/ .

title: Guide 01 · Encoder–Decoder Architectures
text:
Encoder–Decoder Architectures for Industrial Segmentation 
 In Milestone 2, you assembled a foundational segmentation pipeline: feeding line-scan strips through a basic convolutional network, thresholding probabilities, and packaging predictions into run-length encodings. However, industrial anomaly detection poses a severe spatial paradox:  how can a neural network capture global contextual information across an  \(800\) -pixel wide steel sheet while simultaneously preserving the sub-millimeter edge boundaries of a 2-pixel wide hairline scratch? 
 Standard classification networks solve recognition by discarding spatial resolution through pooling and strided convolutions. If you apply that strategy directly to segmentation, boundary localization is permanently destroyed. 
 This guide explores the architectural engine designed to resolve this paradox: the  encoder–decoder network with lateral skip connections . You will learn how feature hierarchies contract and expand, trace exact tensor shapes through an anisotropic industrial strip ( \(128 \times 800\) ), dissect the mathematical differences between skip concatenation and addition, and diagnose spatial misalignment bugs before they degrade your validation scores. 
 
 1. The Spatial Dilemma: Why Classification Features Cannot Segment 
 To understand why segmentation models require a two-part architecture, consider what happens inside a standard image classification model (such as an ImageNet classifier): 
 Classification Paradigm (Translation Invariant):
Input [1, 128, 800] ──► Downsample (32×) ──► Global Average Pooling ──► Class Vector [C]
                                              (All spatial coordinates destroyed!) 
 Classification networks are deliberately engineered to be  translation invariant : whether an inclusion defect sits at the far left edge ( \(x=12\) ) or near the center ( \(x=400\) ), the classification label is still  "defect_c" . To achieve this invariance, the network repeatedly pools features, expanding the receptive field until each neuron summarizes the entire image into a 1D vector. 
 In contrast, semantic segmentation is fundamentally  translation equivariant : if a scratch shifts 10 pixels to the right, the predicted mask must shift by exactly 10 pixels to the right. Global pooling is fatal to segmentation because spatial coordinates  \([y, x]\)  cannot be recovered from a single scalar summary. 
 Segmentation Paradigm (Translation Equivariant):
Input [1, 128, 800] ──► Feature Extraction ──► Spatial Reconstruction ──► Pixel Mask [K, 128, 800]
                        (Contracting Path)      (Expanding Path)          (Every pixel localized) 
 To output a pixel-aligned mask, a model must achieve two opposing objectives: 
 
 High Semantic Abstraction : Distinguish true metallurgical anomalies from harmless surface glare, rolling oil stains, and sensor noise (requiring a large receptive field). 
 Millimeter Spatial Precision : Delineate exact defect borders, preserving thin cracks that may span only 1 to 3 pixels in width (requiring high spatial resolution). 
 
 
 2. The Encoder–Decoder Paradigm 
 The universal solution to this dual requirement is the  encoder–decoder architecture  (pioneered by Long et al., 2015 with Fully Convolutional Networks, and refined by Ronneberger et al., 2015 with U-Net). 
 
 Figure 1.1: The Encoder–Decoder architecture for industrial strip segmentation ( \(128 \times 800\) ). The contracting path captures semantic defect context, the expanding path restores spatial dimensions, and lateral skip connections preserve high-frequency boundary details. 
 An encoder–decoder comprises three distinct functional zones: 
 1. The Contracting Path (Encoder) 
 The encoder acts as a hierarchical feature extractor. As input tensors propagate through successive convolutional blocks and downsampling layers (typically  \(2\times 2\)  max pooling or strided convolutions with stride 2): 
 
 Spatial Resolution Decreases : Height and width are progressively halved ( \(H \to H/2 \to H/4 \dots\) ,  \(W \to W/2 \to W/4 \dots\) ). 
 Channel Depth Increases : The number of feature channels grows ( \(1 \to 64 \to 128 \to 256 \to 512\) ). 
 Receptive Field Expands : Early layers respond only to tiny local patches (edges, gradients), whereas deep layers view large regions of the strip (textural irregularities, long structural defects). 
 
 2. The Bottleneck 
 The bottleneck represents the transition point between contraction and expansion. It possesses the  smallest spatial resolution  and the  largest channel capacity  (e.g.,  \(8 \times 50\)  pixels with  \(512\)  channels for a  \(128 \times 800\)  input).
At this stage, spatial coordinate fidelity is at its lowest, but semantic feature density is at its highest. The bottleneck computes global context: it "knows" whether an anomaly exists and what type of surface disruption has occurred, but its spatial boundaries are blurry and coarse. 
 3. The Expanding Path (Decoder) 
 The decoder is responsible for  spatial recovery . Through a sequence of upsampling operators (such as bilinear interpolation or transposed convolutions) paired with convolutional refinement blocks: 
 
 Spatial Resolution Increases : Dimensions are progressively doubled ( \(8 \times 50 \to 16 \times 100 \to 32 \to 64 \to 128 \times 800\) ). 
 Channel Depth Decreases : Feature maps are projected back to manageable channel widths. 
 Output Projection : A final  \(1 \times 1\)  convolution maps the refined feature maps to the desired number of output logits ( \(K\)  channels at  \(128 \times 800\) ). 
 
 
 3. Spatial Mechanics: Tracing an Industrial Strip ( \(128 \times 800\) ) 
 In industrial inspection, images are rarely square. In our line-scan setting, images have an anisotropic resolution of  \(128 \times 800\)  pixels  (aspect ratio  \(6.25:1\) ).

 \[128 / 2^4 = 128 / 16 = 8, \quad 800 / 2^4 = 800 / 16 = 50\] 
 Both dimensions divide cleanly by  \(2^4 = 16\)  (and even by  \(2^5 = 32\) , yielding  \(4 \times 25\) ). There are no fractional spatial boundaries, ensuring that every upsampled feature map matches its corresponding skip connection exactly. 
 
 4. The Spatial Detail Crisis & Skip Connections 
 Why can a decoder not simply upsample bottleneck features using bilinear interpolation without skip connections? 
 Consider a thin longitudinal scratch ( defect_a ) that is  2 pixels wide  on the original canvas: 
 
 At  \(2\times\)  downsampling  ( \(64 \times 400\) ), the crack occupies 1 feature cell. 
 At  \(4\times\)  downsampling  ( \(32 \times 200\) ), the crack occupies  \(0.5\)  feature cells. The signal blurs into the surrounding background pixels. 
 At  \(16\times\)  downsampling  ( \(8 \times 50\) ), a single feature cell corresponds to a  \(16 \times 16 = 256\)  pixel patch of the physical steel sheet. The 2-pixel wide scratch represents less than  \(1\%\)  of the spatial energy in that cell! 
 
 Physical Defect Cross-Section Across Contracting Stages:
Stage 0 (Input 1×):        [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]  <-- 2 pixels wide, perfectly distinct
Stage 1 (Downsampled 2×):  [0, 0, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0, 0] <-- Boundary begins to spread
Stage 2 (Downsampled 4×):  [0, 0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 0]     <-- Sub-pixel blurring
Stage 4 (Bottleneck 16×):  [0.05, 0.05]              <-- Spatial boundary dissolved into average 
 When the decoder attempts to upsample from  \(8 \times 50\)  back to  \(128 \times 800\) , standard bilinear interpolation can only create smooth, blurry gradients. It cannot recreate the sharp high-frequency edge of the 2-pixel crack because that information was mathematically destroyed during pooling. 
 The Skip Connection Solution 
 Skip connections  bridge this information gap. They take the high-resolution feature maps generated in the early encoder stages (before pooling occurs) and route them directly across to the corresponding decoder stage. 
 When the decoder combines upsampled contextual features with early skip features: 
 
 The upsampled features provide the answer to:  "Is this an anomaly, and what type is it?" 
 The skip features provide the answer to:  "Where exactly is the physical boundary of this anomaly?" 
 
 
 5. Skip Fusion Mechanics: Concatenation vs. Addition 
 How should the decoder merge the skip feature map  \(X_{\text{skip}}\)  with the upsampled feature map  \(X_{\text{up}}\) ? In modern architectures, two primary fusion mechanisms exist: 
 Mechanism A: Concatenation (U-Net Standard)
X_up   [B, C_up, H, W]   ┐
                         ├─► torch.cat([X_up, X_skip], dim=1) ──► [B, C_up + C_skip, H, W]
X_skip [B, C_skip, H, W] ┘

Mechanism B: Elementwise Addition (ResNet / LinkNet / FPN)
X_up   [B, C, H, W]      ┐
                         ├─► X_up + X_skip ──────────────────────► [B, C, H, W]
X_skip [B, C, H, W]      ┘  (Requires C_up == C_skip) 
 Mathematical Formulation 
 1. Concatenation Fusion 
 \[X_{\text{fused}} = \left[ X_{\text{up}} \;\|\; X_{\text{skip}} \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times (C_{\text{up}} + C_{\text{skip}}) \times H \times W}\] 
 Followed by a convolution layer: 
 \[Y = \text{ReLU}\left( \text{BatchNorm}\left( W * X_{\text{fused}} + b \right) \right)\] 
 
 Mechanism : The feature maps are stacked along the channel axis. 
 Advantage : Preserves distinct representations. The network does not force high-level abstract features and low-level edge features to share the same channel space; the subsequent convolution can learn custom linear combinations of both. 
 Cost : Channel count doubles ( \(C_{\text{up}} + C_{\text{skip}}\) ), increasing GPU VRAM consumption and decoder parameter counts. 
 
 2. Elementwise Addition Fusion 
 \[X_{\text{fused}} = X_{\text{up}} + X_{\text{skip}} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times H \times W}\] 
 
 Mechanism : Corresponding feature cells are summed. 
 Advantage : Highly parameter-efficient and memory-frugal. Channel counts do not expand ( \(C\)  remains constant), reducing memory bandwidth during backpropagation. 
 Cost : Requires strict channel agreement ( \(C_{\text{up}} = C_{\text{skip}}\) ). If channel counts differ, a  \(1 \times 1\)  projection convolution must be applied first. Furthermore, adding feature maps forces the representation spaces to align, potentially overwriting subtle high-frequency signals. 
 
 
 6. Spatial Alignment & Stride Traps: Diagnosing Shape Incompatibilities 
 A common source of silent failure in segmentation is  dimension misalignment . Because segmentation involves multiple downsampling and upsampling operations, an incompatible image dimension or improper padding can cause feature maps to differ by 1 pixel. 
 The Odd-Dimension Hazard 
 Suppose a dataset contains images of dimension  \(H = 125, W = 800\) : 
 
 Input:  \(125 \times 800\) . 
 Level 1 MaxPool (stride 2):  \(\lfloor 125 / 2 \rfloor = 62 \times 400\) . 
 Level 2 MaxPool (stride 2):  \(\lfloor 62 / 2 \rfloor = 31 \times 200\) . 
 Level 3 MaxPool (stride 2):  \(\lfloor 31 / 2 \rfloor = 15 \times 100\) . 
 Decoder Level 3 Upsample ( \(2\times\) ):  \(15 \times 2 = 30 \times 200\) . 
 
 When the decoder attempts to concatenate the upsampled tensor ( \(30 \times 200\) ) with the Level 2 skip connection ( \(31 \times 200\) ), PyTorch throws a fatal error:
 RuntimeError: Sizes of tensors must match except in dimension 1. Expected size 31 but got size 30 for dimension 2. 
 The Dangerous Anti-Pattern: Blind Resizing 
 A frequent student mistake when encountering this runtime error is to insert an ad-hoc resize:
 # DANGEROUS ANTI-PATTERN: DO NOT DO THIS!
d3_upsampled = F.interpolate(d3, size=s2.shape[2:], mode="bilinear") # Silently stretches! 
While this silences the PyTorch exception, it introduces  spatial phase distortion . Bilinear stretching shifts feature coordinates relative to the physical steel canvas. When predictions are mapped back to ground truth, defect edges are systematically misaligned by 1 to 2 pixels, causing severe drops in the Dice score on thin scratches. 
 The Correct Engineering Solution 
 For our competition dataset ( \(128 \times 800\) ), dimensions are powers of two ( \(128 = 2^7, 800 = 2^5 \times 25\) ). If you ever crop or patch your images,  ensure every crop dimension is divisible by  \(2^D\) , where  \(D\)  is the maximum downsampling depth of your architecture (for  \(D=5\) , crops must be multiples of 32). 
 
 7. Simple U-Net vs. Pretrained-Encoder U-Net: A Conceptual Shift 
 In Milestone 2, you explored a basic U-Net where both encoder and decoder were initialized randomly and trained from scratch. In Milestone 3, you make a conceptual transition:  decoupling the feature extractor from the reconstruction engine . 
 Milestone 2 Baseline (Symmetric, From-Scratch):
[Simple Conv Encoder] ──(Skips)──► [Simple Conv Decoder]
(Initialized randomly; must learn edges, textures, and anomalies simultaneously)

Milestone 3 Pretrained Architecture (Asymmetric, Transfer Learning):
[Pretrained Backbone (e.g. ResNet34)] ──(Skips)──► [Task-Specific Decoder]
(Pretrained on 1.2M ImageNet images;                 (Custom decoder tailored to
 rich edge & texture filters ready on Day 1)          industrial strip geometry) 
 In a pretrained encoder–decoder: 
 
 The Encoder is Standardized : We replace custom convolution stacks with proven computer vision backbones (such as  resnet34 ,  efficientnet-b0 , or  convnext ). 
 Feature Taps are Heterogeneous : Unlike a symmetric U-Net where every encoder stage has identical layer counts, pretrained backbones feature asymmetric stage depths and non-uniform channel distributions (e.g., ResNet stages have channels  \(64, 128, 256, 512\) ). 
 The Decoder Adapts to the Backbone : The decoder's skip input channels must be explicitly configured to match the channel output of each tapped backbone stage. 
 
 
 8. Comparative Decision Matrix 
 
 
 
 Architectural Feature 
 Concatenation Skips (U-Net) 
 Addition Skips (FPN / LinkNet) 
 No Skips (Dilated / DeepLab) 
 
 
 
 
 Thin Defect Boundary Fidelity 
 Excellent : Direct routing of raw pixel coordinates. 
 Good : Combines features with minimal distortion. 
 Poor : Coarse boundaries; misses hairline scratches. 
 
 
 GPU Memory Footprint 
 High : Decoder channel counts double at each level. 
 Low : Channel count remains constant. 
 Moderate : Requires atrous spatial pyramid pooling.

 Moderate (governed by downsampling depth). 
 Moderate. 
 Very High : Dilated convolutions expand receptive field without resolution loss. 
 
 
 Recommended Regime 
 Primary baseline for industrial defect segmentation. 
 High-throughput, memory-constrained environments. 
 Large amorphous defects (e.g., broad stains, rolling marks). 
 
 
 
 
 9. Common Implementation Pitfalls and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Diagnostic & Fix 
 
 
 
 
 Channel Axis Mismatch in  torch.cat 
 Concatenating along spatial axis instead of channel axis ( dim=2  instead of  dim=1 ). 
 RuntimeError: Sizes of tensors must match except in dimension 2 . 
 Ensure  torch.cat([up, skip], dim=1)  explicitly specifies channel dimension. 
 
 
 Spatial Off-by-One Mismatch 
 Using an odd spatial crop (e.g.,  \(125 \times 800\) ) with stride-2 pooling. 
 Shape mismatch error during decoder concatenation. 
 Pad input or ensure all dimensions are divisible by  \(2^D\)  ( \(D\)  = downsampling depth). 
 
 
 Receptive Field Starvation 
 Encoder has too few downsampling stages (e.g., only 2 levels,  \(4\times\)  downsampling). 
 Network confuses large textural background patterns with defects; cannot learn global context. 
 Ensure encoder downsamples by at least  \(16\times\)  (down to  \(8 \times 50\) ) at the bottleneck. 
 
 
 Skipping Across Misaligned Scales 
 Routing Stage 1 skip (stride 2) into Decoder Stage 3 (stride 8). 
 Immediate tensor shape mismatch error during forward pass. 
 Construct a systematic shape tracing table (as in Section 3) to verify stage alignment. 
 
 
 
 
 10. Ungraded Try-It Activity: Trace Receptive Field and Tensor Shapes 
 Test your understanding of spatial mechanics with this short paper-and-pencil or scratchpad exercise: 
 Suppose you design a 3-level encoder for a  \(128 \times 800\)  strip image: 
 
 Input: Grayscale strip  \([1, 128, 800]\) . 
 Encoder Block 1: Two  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutions (stride 1, padding 1) followed by MaxPool2d (kernel 2, stride 2). 
 Encoder Block 2: Two  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutions (stride 1, padding 1) followed by MaxPool2d (kernel 2, stride 2). 
 Bottleneck: One  \(3 \times 3\)  convolution (stride 1, padding 1). 
 
 Questions to answer: 
 
 What is the spatial resolution  \([H, W]\)  of the feature map entering the bottleneck? 
 If a defect has a bounding box of  \(4 \times 12\)  pixels on the input strip, what is its maximum spatial footprint (in feature cells) at the bottleneck? 
 If you replace the MaxPool2d in Block 2 with an anisotropic pooling operator  nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=(1, 2), stride=(1, 2)) , what will the bottleneck spatial dimensions be? Why might an engineer consider anisotropic pooling for an  \(800 \times 128\)  strip? 
 
 
 Click here to view the worked solution 
 
 Bottleneck spatial dimensions : 
 After Block 1:  \(128 / 2 = 64\) ,  \(800 / 2 = 400 \to [64, 400]\) . 
 After Block 2:  \(64 / 2 = 32\) ,  \(400 / 2 = 200 \to [32, 200]\) . 
 The bottleneck receives feature maps of shape  \([B, C, 32, 200]\) . 
 
 
 Defect footprint at bottleneck : 
 The total downsampling factor is  \(4\times\)  along both axes. 
 Height:  \(4\text{ px} / 4 = 1\text{ cell}\) . 
 Width:  \(12\text{ px} / 4 = 3\text{ cells}\) . 
 The defect spans at most  \(1 \times 3\)  feature cells. If downsampled by another  \(2\times\)  (total  \(8\times\) ), the height drops to  \(0.5\)  cells and disappears into adjacent background cells. 
 
 
 Anisotropic pooling : 
 Pooling by  \((1, 2)\)  downsamples width by half while keeping height untouched. 
 Resulting bottleneck shape:  \(H = 64 / 1 = 64\) ,  \(W = 400 / 2 = 200 \to [64, 200]\) . 
 Rationale : Industrial strips are very short along the vertical axis ( \(128\text{ px}\) ) but very wide along the horizontal axis ( \(800\text{ px}\) ). Anisotropic pooling prevents the short vertical axis from collapsing too quickly while aggressively downsampling the wide rolling axis! 
 
 
 
 
 To run a complete CPU shape-tracing forward pass on synthetic tensors, inspect:
👉  docs/milestone_3_student_guide/examples/toy_feature_extractor.py 
 
 11. Primary Sources & Further Reading 
 
 Ronneberger, O., Fischer, P., & Brox, T. (2015) .  U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation . MICCAI.  arXiv:1505.04597 . The foundational paper establishing skip connections for dense spatial recovery. 
 Long, J., Shelhamer, E., & Darrell, T. (2015) .  Fully Convolutional Networks for Semantic Segmentation . CVPR.  arXiv:1411.4038 . Introduced the concept of replacing fully connected layers with convolutions for pixel-dense predictions. 
 Lin, T. Y., et al. (2017) .  Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection . CVPR.  arXiv:1612.03144 . Explains top-down pathways and lateral connections for combining multi-scale feature hierarchies.

title: Guide 02 · Pretrained Backbones
text:
Pretrained Backbones & Transfer Learning: ResNet to EfficientNet 
 In Milestone 2, your baseline U-Net was initialized with random Gaussian weights. When trained from scratch, the network faced a difficult optimization task: it had to discover basic visual primitives (such as edge filters, contrast gradients, and texture detectors) while simultaneously learning to identify rare metallurgical defects from a small training dataset. 
 In computer vision, training from scratch on small or imbalanced datasets is rarely optimal.  Transfer learning  allows you to leverage neural networks trained on massive public corpora (such as ImageNet-1k, containing over 1.28 million natural images across 1,000 categories). By adopting a  pretrained backbone  as your encoder, your model begins training with an established visual vocabulary ready on day one. 
 This guide explains what pretrained backbones learn, compares the architectural mechanics of the  ResNet  and  EfficientNet  families, details how decoders extract multi-scale feature hierarchies, examines the trade-offs of feature freezing versus full fine-tuning, and provides a rigorous, controlled experimentation protocol to verify whether transfer learning truly improves your model. 
 
 1. The Transfer Learning Advantage in Industrial Anomaly Detection 
 Why should a neural network trained to identify golden retrievers, freight trains, and espresso makers help you segment microscopic cracks on cold-rolled steel? 
 The answer lies in the  hierarchical nature of visual representations  discovered by deep convolutional networks (Yosinski et al., 2014): 
 Visual Hierarchy in Pretrained CNNs:
Early Layers (Stage 1-2):   General Visual Primitives (Gabor edges, blobs, local gradients)
Mid Layers (Stage 3-4):     Complex Textural Patterns (grain textures, junctions, lattices)
Deep Layers (Stage 5):      High-Level Semantic Motifs (parts, global context, objects) 
 
 Figure 2.1: Multi-scale feature tap points in a pretrained backbone. Early layers supply high-resolution edge maps to the decoder, while deep layers provide semantic anomaly classification. 
 1. General Visual Primitives Are Domain-Agnostic 
 The filters learned in the first two stages of an ImageNet model are almost indistinguishable from classical Gabor wavelets and Sobel gradient operators. They detect high-contrast boundaries, directional ridges, and color/intensity transitions. A hairline scratch on steel triggers the exact same edge-detection neurons as the outline of a violin in ImageNet! 
 2. Feature Reusability with Limited Data 
 In industrial anomaly detection, defect samples are scarce. Anomaly classes like  defect_b  appear in only a tiny fraction of images. A randomly initialized model requires thousands of positive gradient updates just to shape its early convolutional kernels into coherent edge detectors. A pretrained backbone already possesses these detectors, allowing the optimizer to focus its limited updates on learning the subtle textural signatures of anomalies. 
 3. What Parts Are Reused? 
 When repurposing a classification network for segmentation: 
 
 RETAINED : The convolutional stem and all convolutional feature stages (the "body"). 
 DISCARDED : The global average pooling layer, the flattening operator, and the final 1,000-class fully connected classification layer (the "head"). 
 ADDED : A task-specific segmentation decoder that consumes feature maps tapped from multiple intermediate stages of the backbone. 
 
 
 2. Comparing Backbone Families: ResNet vs. EfficientNet 
 Rather than treating backbones as black boxes, you should understand how their internal building blocks differ. Two of the most successful and widely deployed backbone families in competitive segmentation are  ResNet  and  EfficientNet . 
 A. The ResNet Family: Residual Highway Mechanics 
 Introduced by He et al. (2016), the Residual Network (ResNet) family solved the vanishing gradient problem in very deep networks using  identity skip additions . 
 ResNet Residual Block:
x ──┬───────────────────────────────┐ (Identity Shortcut)
    │                               │
    ▼                               ▼
 [Conv 3×3] ──► [BN] ──► [ReLU] ──► [Conv 3×3] ──► [BN] ──► (+) ──► [ReLU] ──► Output 
 Mathematical Formulation 
 \[\mathcal{F}(x) = W_2 \cdot \sigma\left( \text{BN}\left( W_1 \cdot x + b_1 \right) \right) + b_2\] 
 \[y = \sigma\left( \text{BN}\left( \mathcal{F}(x) + x \right) \right)\] 
 Because gradients flow directly through the identity shortcut ( \(+ x\) ) during backpropagation, ResNet avoids gradient degradation even at 100+ layers. 
 Structural Characteristics 
 
 Homogeneous Blocks : Built from uniform sequences of  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutions (or bottleneck blocks  \(1 \times 1 \to 3 \times 3 \to 1 \times 1\)  in ResNet-50 and deeper). 
 Predictable Striding : Consistently downsamples by exactly  \(2\times\)  at the start of each stage ( \(/4, /8, /16, /32\) ). 
 Clean Feature Taps : Feature map channel counts are predictable powers of two:  \(64, 128, 256, 512\)  (ResNet-34) or  \(256, 512, 1024, 2048\)  (ResNet-50). 
 Strengths : Highly stable gradients, low memory overhead per parameter, excellent boundary extraction on high-contrast edge defects (scratches). 
 
 
 B. The EfficientNet Family: Compound Scaling & MBConv 
 Introduced by Tan & Le (2019), the EfficientNet family redesigned backbone architecture through principled  compound scaling , balancing network depth, width, and resolution using neural architecture search. 
 EfficientNet MBConv Block (Inverted Residual + Squeeze-and-Excitation):
x ──┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ (Identity Shortcut)
    │                                                              │
    ▼                                                              ▼
 [1×1 Conv (Expand)] ──► [Depthwise 3×3 Conv] ──► [SE Block] ──► [1×1 Conv (Project)] ──► (+) 
 Key Innovations 
 
 Depthwise Separable Convolutions : Factorizes a standard convolution into a depthwise spatial filter (1 filter per input channel) and a pointwise  \(1 \times 1\)  projection filter across channels. This slashes FLOPs and parameter counts by  \(80\%\text{--}90\%\) . 
 Inverted Residuals : Unlike ResNet (which compresses channels before convolution), MBConv  expands  channel dimensions internally ( \(6\times\)  expansion) to compute rich non-linear representations in high-dimensional space before projecting back down. 
 
 Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) Attention : Applies explicit channel-wise recalibration. A global average pooling step computes channel descriptors, followed by a two-layer bottleneck MLP that outputs per-channel scaling weights  \(s_c \in [0, 1]\) : 
 \[s = \sigma\left( W_2 \cdot \text{ReLU}\left( W_1 \cdot \text{GAP}(x) \right) \right), \quad \tilde{x}_c = s_c \cdot x_c\] 
 This allows the network to dynamically amplify feature channels that correspond to anomaly textures while dampening channels that capture normal background sheen. 
 
 
 Structural Characteristics 
 
 High Parameter Efficiency : EfficientNet-B0 has only  \(\sim 5.3\text{M}\)  parameters compared to ResNet-34's  \(\sim 21.3\text{M}\) , yet achieves comparable or higher ImageNet accuracy. 
 Heterogeneous Channels : Channel counts across stages do not follow strict powers of two (e.g., EfficientNet-B2 outputs stage channels of  \(16, 24, 48, 120, 352\) ). 
 Strengths : High semantic expressiveness per parameter, strong at capturing subtle texture variations (such as metallurgical inclusions or patchy stains). 
 Costs : Slower training throughput on certain GPUs due to the fragmented memory access patterns of depthwise convolutions. 
 
 
 Comparison of ResNet and EfficientNet Variants

 Note: Do not assume one backbone is universally superior for this competition. Your choice must be justified through controlled validation experiments on industrial strip data. 
 
 3. How Decoders Consume Multi-Scale Feature Taps 
 In modern segmentation libraries like  segmentation_models_pytorch  (SMP), a pretrained backbone is sliced into intermediate feature stages.  
 Consider an industrial strip input  \([B, C_{\text{in}}, 128, 800]\)  fed into a ResNet-34 backbone: 
 Backbone Slicing & Feature Tap Output:
Input:           [B, C_in, 128, 800]
  │
  ├─► Stem (Conv1 + MaxPool) ──► Tap 1: [B, 64,  32, 200]  (Stride /4)  ──► Decoder Level 1 Skip
  ├─► Stage 1 (Layer 1)      ──► Tap 2: [B, 64,  32, 200]  (Stride /4)
  ├─► Stage 2 (Layer 2)      ──► Tap 3: [B, 128, 16, 100]  (Stride /8)  ──► Decoder Level 2 Skip
  ├─► Stage 3 (Layer 3)      ──► Tap 4: [B, 256,  8,  50]  (Stride /16) ──► Decoder Level 3 Skip
  └─► Stage 4 (Layer 4)      ──► Tap 5: [B, 512,  4,  25]  (Stride /32) ──► Bottleneck Input 
 When connecting a decoder (such as a U-Net or FPN decoder) to these tap points: 
 
 The Bottleneck  receives Tap 5 ( \(4 \times 25\)  pixels,  \(512\)  channels) and refines the most abstract semantic features. 
 Decoder Upsampling Blocks  progressively double spatial dimensions: 
 \(4 \times 25 \to 8 \times 50\) , concatenated with Tap 4 ( \(256\)  channels). 
 \(8 \times 50 \to 16 \times 100\) , concatenated with Tap 3 ( \(128\)  channels). 
 \(16 \times 100 \to 32 \times 200\) , concatenated with Tap 2 ( \(64\)  channels). 
 \(32 \times 200 \to 128 \times 800\) , restored via final upsampling convolutions to match original strip resolution. 
 
 
 
 Notice that because the backbone downsamples by  \(32\times\) , the input dimensions ( \(128 \times 800\) ) must be cleanly divisible by 32: 
 \[128 / 32 = 4, \quad 800 / 32 = 25\] 
 Both resolve to clean integer grid sizes without fractional truncation! 
 
 4. Fine-Tuning Strategies: Freezing vs. Full Fine-Tuning 
 When applying a pretrained backbone, you must decide how to update its parameters during training. Three strategies exist: 
 Strategy 1: Frozen Feature Extractor (Linear Probing)
Backbone Weights:  FROZEN (requires_grad = False)
Decoder Weights:   TRAINABLE (requires_grad = True)

Strategy 2: Full Fine-Tuning (End-to-End)
Backbone Weights:  TRAINABLE with Global LR
Decoder Weights:   TRAINABLE with Global LR

Strategy 3: Discriminative Learning Rates (Differential Fine-Tuning)
Backbone Weights:  TRAINABLE with Low LR (e.g. 1e-4)
Decoder Weights:   TRAINABLE with High LR (e.g. 1e-3) 
 Trade-Off Analysis 
 
 
 
 Strategy 
 Computational Cost 
 Risk of Catastrophic Forgetting 
 Domain Adaptation Ability 
 Best Use Case 
 
 
 
 
 Frozen Backbone 
 Lowest : No backward gradients computed for backbone. 
 Zero : Pretrained features remain intact. 
 Very Poor : Cannot adapt edge/texture filters to industrial surface physics. 
 Initial pipeline smoke tests or rapid prototyping. 
 
 
 Full Fine-Tuning 
 Standard. 
 Moderate : Large initial gradients from random decoder can disrupt pretrained filters. 
 High : Entire network adapts to strip anomalies. 
 Standard baseline; use learning rate warmup to protect backbone. 
 
 
 Discriminative LR 
 Standard. 
 Low : Backbone updates slowly while decoder learns rapidly. 
 Highest : Preserves general filters while refining domain specifics. 
 Advanced fine-tuning once baseline is established. 
 
 
 
 The Role of Learning Rate Warmup 
 When training starts, the decoder is randomly initialized, producing massive random errors and chaotic gradients. If you apply full fine-tuning with a large initial learning rate, those chaotic gradients propagate back into the backbone and  corrupt the pretrained weights in the very first epoch .
To prevent this, use a  learning rate warmup : start with a small learning rate (e.g.,  \(10\%\text{--}20\%\)  of peak LR) for the first 2 to 3 epochs, allowing the decoder to stabilize before subjecting the backbone to large gradient updates. 
 
 5. Batch Normalization Behavior in Fine-Tuning 
 Batch Normalization ( BatchNorm2d ) is one of the most common sources of subtle bugs when fine-tuning pretrained vision models. 
 During ImageNet pretraining,  BatchNorm  computes running estimates of mean  \(\mu\)  and variance  \(\sigma^2\)  across millions of images with mini-batch sizes of 256 or 512. 
 When you fine-tune on high-resolution industrial strips ( \(128 \times 800\) ), GPU memory constraints often force you to train with  small mini-batch sizes  (such as batch size 4 or 8 per GPU): 
 
 The Small Batch Instability : In mini-batches of size 4, the batch mean and variance fluctuate wildly. If BatchNorm recalculates statistics dynamically, noisy batch statistics destabilize the pretrained feature maps. 
 Eval Mode Freezing ( track_running_stats=False ) : When training with very small batches, some practitioners freeze BatchNorm layers in evaluation mode ( layer.eval() ), forcing the network to use the stable running statistics learned from ImageNet rather than noisy local batch statistics. 
 
 
 6. Preprocessing Compatibility: Normalization Alignment 
 Pretrained backbones are calibrated to expect inputs normalized according to the distribution of their original pretraining dataset. 
 ImageNet Standard Statistics 
 Most torchvision and SMP backbones expect inputs normalized by: 
 \[\mu_{\text{ImageNet}} = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], \quad \sigma_{\text{ImageNet}} = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]\] 
 \[x_{\text{norm}} = \frac{x / 255.0 - \mu}{\sigma}\] 
 The Local Dataset Z-Score Dilemma 
 In industrial steel inspection, line-scan images may have very different brightness distributions (e.g., dark steel surfaces with mean  \(0.35\)  and standard deviation  \(0.12\) ).
If you normalize your input strips using local z-score normalization ( \(\mu_{\text{strip}}, \sigma_{\text{strip}}\) ), the input features will have zero mean and unit variance, but will not match the input scale expected by the first convolutional layer of the pretrained network. 
 Rule of Thumb : 
 
 If using  pretrained weights without an input adapter , apply the backbone's official ImageNet normalization statistics. 
 If using  local per-image z-score normalization , ensure the model's first layer has sufficient learning capacity to rescale the inputs, or train with an explicit input normalization layer. 
 
 
 7. Controlled Backbone Comparison Protocol 
 When experimenting with backbones, you must ensure that performance differences reflect true architectural advantages rather than confounding variables. 
 Controlled Comparison Protocol:
Fix: Validation Split (Canonical Fold 0)
Fix: Input Resolution (Native 128 × 800)
Fix: Output Head & Target Semantics (e.g. 4-Sigmoid, Multi-Label)
Fix: Loss Function (e.g. BCE + Soft Dice, alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
Fix: Optimization Budget (30 Epochs, AdamW, Cosine Scheduler, Batch Size 16)
Fix: Evaluation Pipeline (Same threshold sweep tau in [0.3..0.8], same Dice metric)

Vary ONLY the Backbone:
Experiment A: From-Scratch Baseline (Random Weights)
Experiment B: Pretrained ResNet-34 (ImageNet Weights)
Experiment C: Pretrained EfficientNet-B0 (ImageNet Weights)
Experiment D: Pretrained EfficientNet-B2 (ImageNet Weights) 
 By keeping all other factors identical, any difference in validation Dice score directly measures the empirical benefit of that specific backbone. 
 
 8. Common Implementation Pitfalls and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Corrupted Pretrained Weights 
 Setting learning rate too high without warmup on epoch 1. 
 Training loss spikes to  NaN  or plateaus immediately; validation score drops below random init. 
 Add a 2-epoch linear LR warmup; inspect first-epoch gradient norms. 
 
 
 Mismatched Normalization 
 Feeding raw  \([0, 255]\)  integer pixels into a pretrained backbone expecting normalized  \([-2, +2]\)  floats. 
 Activations saturate; gradients vanish in early layers. 
 Check  image.min()  and  image.max()  before model forward pass. 
 
 
 Decoder Channel Misconfiguration 
 Hardcoding decoder skip channels assuming ResNet, then swapping to EfficientNet. 
 RuntimeError: Given groups=1, weight of size [128, 64, 3, 3], expected input to have 64 channels, but got 48 channels . 
 Use high-level model factories (such as SMP) that automatically configure decoder skip channels from the backbone metadata. 
 
 
 Evaluating with  model.train() 
 Running validation loop without calling  model.eval() . 
 Validation Dice fluctuates wildly across identical evaluation batches due to running batch norm updates. 
 Explicitly call  model.eval()  and  with torch.no_grad():  during validation. 
 
 
 
 
 9. Ungraded Try-It Activity: Inspecting Backbone Feature Activations 
 Try this conceptual calculation: 
 Suppose you pass a  \(128 \times 800\)  strip through a ResNet-34 encoder. 
 
 Recall the stage downsampling factors: Stage 1 ( \(4\times\) ), Stage 2 ( \(8\times\) ), Stage 3 ( \(16\times\) ), Stage 4 ( \(32\times\) ). 
 What are the spatial dimensions  \([H, W]\)  at each of the 4 stages? 
 Calculate the total number of spatial feature cells ( \(H \times W\) ) at Stage 1 vs. Stage 4. 
 If a scratch has length  \(200\text{ px}\)  along the horizontal rolling axis: 
 How many cells does it span at Stage 1? 
 How many cells does it span at Stage 4? 
 
 
 
 
 Click here to view the worked solution 
 
 Spatial dimensions : 
 Stage 1 ( \(4\times\)  downsampling):  \(128 / 4 = 32\) ,  \(800 / 4 = 200 \to [32, 200]\) . 
 Stage 2 ( \(8\times\)  downsampling):  \(128 / 8 = 16\) ,  \(800 / 8 = 100 \to [16, 100]\) . 
 Stage 3 ( \(16\times\)  downsampling):  \(128 / 16 = 8\) ,  \(800 / 16 = 50 \to [8, 50]\) . 
 Stage 4 ( \(32\times\)  downsampling):  \(128 / 32 = 4\) ,  \(800 / 32 = 25 \to [4, 25]\) . 
 
 
 Total spatial feature cells : 
 Stage 1:  \(32 \times 200 = 6,400\text{ cells}\) . 
 Stage 4:  \(4 \times 25 = 100\text{ cells}\) . 
 Spatial resolution decreases by a factor of  \(64\times\)  ( \(6400 / 100 = 64\) )! 
 
 
 Scratch footprint : 
 Stage 1:  \(200 / 4 = 50\text{ cells}\)  along the horizontal axis. The network has plenty of spatial granularity to track curved trajectories and localized breaks. 
 Stage 4:  \(200 / 32 = 6.25\text{ cells}\) . The entire  \(200\) -pixel scratch is compressed into roughly 6 cells, providing global context but coarse localization. 
 
 
 
 
 To verify how multi-scale feature maps are extracted and passed through skip connections on CPU, run:
👉  docs/milestone_3_student_guide/examples/toy_feature_extractor.py 
 
 10. Primary Sources & Further Reading 
 
 He, K., Zhang, X., Ren, S., & Sun, J. (2016) .  Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition . CVPR.  arXiv:1512.03385 . Introduced ResNet and residual learning. 
 Tan, M., & Le, Q. V. (2019) .  EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks . ICML.  arXiv:1905.11946 . Formulated compound scaling and inverted bottleneck architecture. 
 Yosinski, J., Clune, J., Bengio, Y., & Lipson, H. (2014) .  How transferable are features in deep neural networks? . NeurIPS.  arXiv:1411.1792 . Empirical investigation into feature generality across layers. 
 Hu, J., Shen, L., & Sun, G. (2018) .  Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks . CVPR.  arXiv:1709.01507 . Introduced channel attention recalibration used in EfficientNet.

title: Guide 03 · Grayscale Input Adaptation
text:
Adapting Pretrained RGB Backbones to Single-Channel Grayscale 
 When you initialize a computer vision backbone from an ImageNet checkpoint (such as a ResNet or an EfficientNet), the network arrives with an uncompromising architectural contract:  it expects 3-channel RGB image tensors : 
 \[\text{Input Tensor} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times H \times W}\] 
 However, industrial surface anomaly inspection takes place under monochromatic illumination. High-speed industrial line-scan cameras capture intensity strips containing  only 1 grayscale channel : 
 \[\text{Grayscale Strip} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1 \times 128 \times 800}\] 
 If you attempt to feed a 1-channel tensor directly into an off-the-shelf ImageNet backbone, PyTorch will halt with an immediate shape incompatibility error:
 RuntimeError: Given groups=1, weight of size [64, 3, 7, 7], expected input[1, 1, 128, 800] to have 3 channels, but got 1 channels instead. 
 How should you bridge this architectural mismatch? Repeating the channel? Modifying the first convolution layer? Or prepending a learned projection adapter? 
 This guide examines  three defensible grayscale adaptation strategies , proves their mathematical relationships, analyzes their impact on GPU memory and normalization physics, and equips you to make a principled choice for your pipeline. 
 
 1. The Core Dilemma: Color Channels vs. Monochromatic Physics 
 Before examining code, consider what color channels mean to a convolutional neural network. 
 In natural image photography (ImageNet), red, green, and blue channels represent distinct spectral wavelengths: 
 
 A ripe tomato has high red values and low green/blue values. 
 The sky has high blue values and low red values. 
 Pretrained first-layer filters (often  \(7 \times 7\)  kernels in ResNet or  \(3 \times 3\)  in EfficientNet) have learned  color-opponent receptive fields  (e.g., green-magenta or blue-yellow transitions) as well as  achromatic luminance edge detectors . 
 
 In industrial steel manufacturing, there is no chromatic variation. The surface of a cold-rolled steel strip is entirely monochromatic: 
 
 Rolling marks, scratches, scale inclusions, and oil spots are defined strictly by  photometric intensity variations  (darker or lighter shades of gray) and  spatial micro-textures . 
 Repeating a grayscale channel three times does not create color information . It simply feeds three identical copies of the monochromatic signal into the three RGB input sockets of the network. 
 
 
 Figure 3.1: The three architectural strategies for adapting a 3-channel pretrained backbone to single-channel industrial strips. Each strategy offers different trade-offs in GPU memory, parameter overhead, and implementation complexity. 
 
 2. Strategy 1: Channel Duplication ( \(1 \to 3\)  Repeat) 
 The simplest and most common approach in competitive computer vision is  channel duplication : replicating the single grayscale channel across all three input channels before passing it to the backbone. 
 Implementation Mechanics 
 In PyTorch, duplication is performed either in the  DataLoader  or at the start of the model's  forward()  method: 
 # In Dataset / DataLoader:
image_rgb = np.repeat(image_gray, 3, axis=0)  # Shape: [3, 128, 800]

# Or inside PyTorch Model forward():
def forward(self, x_gray):
    # x_gray shape: [B, 1, 128, 800]
    x_rgb = x_gray.repeat(1, 3, 1, 1)        # Shape: [B, 3, 128, 800]
    return self.backbone(x_rgb) 
 Mathematical Filter Response 
 Let  \(x\)  be a single-channel grayscale image patch. The first convolution layer possesses weights  \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}} \times 3 \times K \times K}\)  with filter slices  \(W_{\text{R}}, W_{\text{G}}, W_{\text{B}}\)  and bias  \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}}}\) . 
 When the duplicated input is convolved with filter  \(W\) : 
 \[\text{Output} = W_{\text{R}} * x + W_{\text{G}} * x + W_{\text{B}} * x + b = \left( W_{\text{R}} + W_{\text{G}} + W_{\text{B}} \right) * x + b\] 
 Each output feature cell simply computes the  sum of the three color filter slices  convolved with the grayscale patch! 
 Trade-Offs 
 
 Advantages : 
 Zero parameter changes : The pretrained backbone is preserved in its exact original state. 
 Zero weight modification bugs : Pretrained weights load seamlessly without custom checkpoint manipulation. 
 
 
 Disadvantages : 
 Memory Overhead : Input tensors occupy  \(3\times\)  the memory in RAM, DataLoader inter-process communication (IPC), and GPU VRAM before the first layer. 
 Compute Inefficiency : The first convolutional layer executes  \(3\times\)  more multiplication and addition operations than strictly necessary. 
 
 
 
 
 3. Strategy 2: First-Layer Convolution Modification ( \(3 \to 1\)  Weight Collapse) 
 Instead of inflating the input data to fit the model,  Strategy 2 modifies the model's first convolutional layer to fit the data . 
 We replace the initial 3-channel convolution with a 1-channel convolution: 
 \[\text{Original Conv: } \text{Conv2d}(3, 64, \text{kernel}=7) \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{Adapted Conv: } \text{Conv2d}(1, 64, \text{kernel}=7)\] 
 The challenge is:  how should the new 1-channel weights  \(W_{\text{new}} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 1 \times 7 \times 7}\)  be initialized from the pretrained RGB weights  \(W_{\text{orig}} \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 3 \times 7 \times 7}\) ? 
 Two primary mathematical formulations exist: 
 A. Weight Summing ( \(W_{\text{new}} = W_{\text{R}} + W_{\text{G}} + W_{\text{B}}\) ) 
 \[W_{\text{new}}[c, 0, :, :] = \sum_{j=0}^{2} W_{\text{orig}}[c, j, :, :]\] 
 
 
 Mathematical Property : As proven in Section 2, summing the three filter slices produces the  exact same numerical activation output  as repeating the input across three channels: 
 \[\text{Output}_{\text{sum}} = \left( \sum_{j} W_j \right) * x + b \equiv W_{\text{orig}} * [x, x, x]^T + b\] 
 
 
 This guarantees  \(100\%\)  mathematical equivalence to Strategy 1 without storing or transferring 3-channel tensors! 
 
 
 B. Weight Averaging ( \(W_{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{3} (W_{\text{R}} + W_{\text{G}} + W_{\text{B}})\) ) 
 \[W_{\text{new}}[c, 0, :, :] = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{j=0}^{2} W_{\text{orig}}[c, j, :, :]\] 
 
 Mathematical Property : Averaging divides the sum by 3. 
 Why do some engineers prefer averaging?  In natural RGB images, the red, green, and blue channels have variance  \(\sigma^2\)  but are not perfectly correlated. In grayscale duplication, all three channels have correlation  \(r = 1.0\) . If a filter was trained assuming uncorrelated inputs, summing can increase the variance of the first-layer activations by up to  \(3\times\) . Averaging dampens the activation magnitude, keeping the activation distribution closer to standard variance. 
 Note : Subsequent Batch Normalization layers will automatically rescale and re-center activations during training, diminishing this difference after a few training epochs. 
 
 Implementation Code Pattern 
 import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def adapt_conv1_to_grayscale(conv1_rgb: nn.Conv2d, mode: str = "sum") -> nn.Conv2d:
    """Adapts a pretrained 3-channel Conv2d layer to accept 1-channel grayscale inputs."""
    out_channels = conv1_rgb.out_channels
    kernel_size = conv1_rgb.kernel_size
    stride = conv1_rgb.stride
    padding = conv1_rgb.padding
    bias = conv1_rgb.bias is not None

    # Instantiate new 1-channel Conv2d
    conv1_gray = nn.Conv2d(
        in_channels=1,
        out_channels=out_channels,
        kernel_size=kernel_size,
        stride=stride,
        padding=padding,
        bias=bias,
    )

    with torch.no_grad():
        w_rgb = conv1_rgb.weight.data  # Shape: [out_ch, 3, k, k]
        if mode == "sum":
            conv1_gray.weight.data = w_rgb.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
        elif mode == "average":
            conv1_gray.weight.data = w_rgb.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown mode: {mode}")

        if bias:
            conv1_gray.bias.data = conv1_rgb.bias.data.clone()

    return conv1_gray 
 Trade-Offs 
 
 Advantages : 
 Memory and Compute Optimal : The entire pipeline operates on native  \([B, 1, 128, 800]\)  tensors. 
 No Data Duplication : Saves bandwidth in CPU-to-GPU memory copies and DataLoader workers. 
 
 
 Disadvantages : 
 State Dict Incompatibility : The model's state dictionary key  conv1.weight  now has shape  [64, 1, 7, 7]  instead of  [64, 3, 7, 7] . If you attempt to load a raw ImageNet checkpoint without adapting the keys, PyTorch will raise a  size mismatch  exception. 
 
 
 
 
 3. Strategy 3: Learned  \(1 \to 3\)  Input Adapter 
 A third defensible architecture is to insert a  small learned projection layer  immediately before the pretrained backbone: 
 Strategy 3 Architecture:
Grayscale Input [B, 1, 128, 800] ──► [Adapter: 1×1 Conv (1 -> 3)] ──► RGB Tensor [B, 3, 128, 800] ──► Pretrained Backbone 
 Implementation Mechanics 
 class GrayscaleAdapterModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, pretrained_backbone):
        super().__init__()
        # 1x1 convolution mapping 1 channel to 3 channels without bias
        self.adapter = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=3, kernel_size=1, bias=False)
        # Initialize adapter weights to 1.0 (equivalent to 3x repeat)
        nn.init.constant_(self.adapter.weight, 1.0)
        self.backbone = pretrained_backbone

    def forward(self, x_gray):
        x_adapted = self.adapter(x_gray)  # Learns optimal linear projection to RGB space
        return self.backbone(x_adapted) 
 Mathematical Interpretation 
 The adapter learns three scalar weights:  \(w_{\text{R}}, w_{\text{G}}, w_{\text{B}}\) .
During forward propagation: 
 \[x_{\text{R}} = w_{\text{R}} \cdot x_{\text{gray}}, \quad x_{\text{G}} = w_{\text{G}} \cdot x_{\text{gray}}, \quad x_{\text{B}} = w_{\text{B}} \cdot x_{\text{gray}}\] 
 Instead of forcing the network to treat red, green, and blue equally, the optimizer can learn to weight the three channels differently, allowing the backbone to favor whichever color filter pathways are most sensitive to surface texture anomalies. 
 Trade-Offs 
 
 Advantages : 
 Keeps the pretrained backbone completely pristine and unmodified. 
 Adds only  3 trainable parameters  ( \(3 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 = 3\)  weights). 
 
 
 Disadvantages : 
 Still produces an intermediate 3-channel feature map in GPU memory. 
 
 
 
 
 4. Normalization Physics: ImageNet Statistics vs. Local Z-Score 
 Regardless of which adaptation strategy you choose, you must address  input normalization . 
 Vision backbones expect inputs normalized according to the channel statistics of ImageNet: 
 \[\mu_{\text{ImageNet}} = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], \quad \sigma_{\text{ImageNet}} = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]\] 
 The Single-Channel Normalization Question 
 If you duplicate a grayscale image  \(x \in [0, 1]\)  into three channels and apply ImageNet normalization: 
 \[x_{\text{norm}, 0} = \frac{x - 0.485}{0.229}, \quad x_{\text{norm}, 1} = \frac{x - 0.456}{0.224}, \quad x_{\text{norm}, 2} = \frac{x - 0.406}{0.225}\] 
 Notice a subtle phenomenon:  the three channels are no longer identical! 
Because the ImageNet channel means and standard deviations differ slightly across R, G, and B, applying ImageNet normalization transforms identical grayscale pixels into three slightly shifted channels: 
 
 Channel 0 (Red) receives an offset of  \(-0.485 / 0.229 = -2.118\) . 
 Channel 1 (Green) receives an offset of  \(-0.456 / 0.224 = -2.036\) . 
 Channel 2 (Blue) receives an offset of  \(-0.406 / 0.225 = -1.804\) . 
 
 What If You Use Local Dataset Z-Score Normalization? 
 Many segmentation practitioners normalize each image individually using its own sample statistics: 
 \[x_{\text{zscore}} = \frac{x - \mu_{\text{strip}}}{\sigma_{\text{strip}} + \epsilon}\] 
 
 Advantage : Eliminates camera lighting drift and exposure differences between different inspection cameras. 
 Pretrained Caution : The resulting values have mean 0.0 and variance 1.0. This does not match ImageNet's normalized distribution. If you use local z-scores, you  must allow the first layer (or the input adapter) to fine-tune  so the network can adjust its bias terms to accommodate the shifted mean. 
 
 
 5. Comparative Decision Matrix

 6. Common Implementation Pitfalls and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Diagnostic & Fix 
 
 
 
 
 Random Re-Initialization of Conv1 
 Replacing  conv1  with  nn.Conv2d(1, 64, ...)  without copying pretrained weights. 
 Model trains significantly slower; early validation Dice is much lower than Strategy 1. 
 Verify that  conv1.weight  is populated using  w_rgb.sum(dim=1)  or  w_rgb.mean(dim=1) . 
 
 
 Channel Axis Mismatch in Repeat 
 Using  x.repeat(3, 1, 1, 1)  instead of  x.repeat(1, 3, 1, 1) . 
 Batch size becomes  \(3B\) , causing immediate batch dimension errors. 
 Assert  x_rep.shape == (B, 3, H, W)  after duplication. 
 
 
 State Dict Key Collision on Resume 
 Loading an unmodified 3-channel checkpoint into an adapted 1-channel model. 
 RuntimeError: Error(s) in loading state_dict: size mismatch for conv1.weight .

 Scale Shock from Zero Initialization 
 Initializing learned adapter weights to zero ( nn.init.zeros_ ). 
 Gradients vanish on forward pass 1; initial loss is completely flat. 
 Initialize adapter weights to  1.0  or  1/3 . 
 
 
 
 
 7. Ungraded Try-It Activity: Verify Activation Equivalence by Hand 
 Work through this small numerical calculation to confirm why weight summing matches channel repetition: 
 Suppose you have a tiny  \(1 \times 1\)  image patch where the grayscale pixel value is  \(x = 2.0\) .
A 3-channel convolution has three weights and a bias: 
 \[W_{\text{R}} = 0.5, \quad W_{\text{G}} = -0.2, \quad W_{\text{B}} = 0.8, \quad b = 0.1\] 
 
 
 Calculate the output using  Strategy 1 (Repeat 3×) : 
 \[x_{\text{in}} = [2.0, 2.0, 2.0]^T\] 
 \[\text{Output}_1 = W_{\text{R}} \cdot x_{\text{in}}[0] + W_{\text{G}} \cdot x_{\text{in}}[1] + W_{\text{B}} \cdot x_{\text{in}}[2] + b\] 
 
 
 Calculate the adapted weight  \(W_{\text{new}}\)  using  Strategy 2 (Summing) : 
 \[W_{\text{new}} = W_{\text{R}} + W_{\text{G}} + W_{\text{B}}\] 
 \[\text{Output}_2 = W_{\text{new}} \cdot x + b\] 
 
 
 Do the two outputs match? 
 
 What would the output be under  Strategy 2 (Averaging) ? How does it differ? 
 
 
 Click here to view the worked solution 
 
 
 Strategy 1 (Repeat 3×) : 
 \[\text{Output}_1 = 0.5(2.0) + (-0.2)(2.0) + 0.8(2.0) + 0.1 = 1.0 - 0.4 + 1.6 + 0.1 = 2.30\] 
 
 
 Strategy 2 (Summing) : 
 \[W_{\text{new}} = 0.5 + (-0.2) + 0.8 = 1.10\] 
 \[\text{Output}_2 = 1.10(2.0) + 0.1 = 2.20 + 0.1 = 2.30\] 
 \[\text{Output}_1 \equiv \text{Output}_2 \text{ (Exact Equality!)}\] 
 
 
 Matching Confirmation :
   Yes, they match identically down to the last decimal place ( \(2.30\) ). 
 
 
 Strategy 2 (Averaging) : 
 \[W_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1.10}{3} \approx 0.3667\] 
 \[\text{Output}_{\text{avg}} = 0.3667(2.0) + 0.1 = 0.7333 + 0.1 = 0.8333\] 
 Notice that the activation magnitude before bias is scaled down by exactly a factor of 3 ( \(2.20 / 3 = 0.7333\) ).
