title: Guide 04 · Output Heads & Semantics
text:
Output Heads & Target Semantics: Multi-Label Sigmoid vs. Multi-Class Softmax 
 In deep learning segmentation, the final layer of your network—the  output head —translates high-level spatial feature maps into class predictions. While this layer is often just a simple  \(1 \times 1\)  convolution, your architectural choices here dictate  your target representation, your activation function, your loss formulation, and your post-processing decision pipeline . 
 In this competition, students frequently debate two competing formulations: 
 
 The 4-Channel Multi-Label Formulation : Four independent binary defect channels activated by  Sigmoid . 
 The 5-Channel Multi-Class Formulation : A background-inclusive categorical partition activated by  Softmax . 
 
 Does one formulation hold a universal theoretical advantage? What happens if two defect classes occur on the same image? And how can you verify whether ground truth annotations physically overlap before committing to an architecture? 
 This guide examines both output heads in detail. You will trace tensor flows through both pipelines, walk through a concrete numerical demonstration of a competing-defect pixel, conduct a rigorous  pixel-level mask overlap audit , analyze the risk of permanent information loss, and learn how to resolve multi-channel predictions at test time. 
 
 1. Two Competing Paradigms: Architectures and Contracts 
 Every output head requires strict mathematical consistency between five components:  output tensor shape, activation function, target tensor encoding, loss function, and inference decision rule . Mixing components across paradigms leads to fatal training failures or silent metric degradation. 
 
 Figure 4.1: The 4-Channel Multi-Label Sigmoid head vs. the 5-Channel Multi-Class Softmax head. Sigmoid evaluates each defect channel independently, while Softmax enforces mutual exclusivity across classes. 
 Paradigm A: The 4-Channel Multi-Label Sigmoid Head 
 In this formulation, the model treats each defect type as an independent binary detection task. 
 Paradigm A Pipeline:
Decoder Features [B, C, H, W]
  │
  ▼
1×1 Conv Head ──► Raw Logits Z: [B, 4, 128, 800]  (Unbounded in (-∞, +∞))
  │
  ├─► Training Flow:   Fed directly to nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() against Binary Target Y: [B, 4, 128, 800]
  │
  └─► Inference Flow:  P_k = σ(z_k) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z_k)) ──► Threshold τ ──► Binary Mask M_k ∈ {0, 1} 
 
 Output Tensor :  \([B, 4, 128, 800]\)  representing defect channels  \([a, b, c, d]\) . There is  no explicit background channel ; background is implicitly represented when all four channels equal 0. 
 Target Tensor :  \([B, 4, 128, 800]\)  float32 tensor with binary values  \(\{0.0, 1.0\}\) . 
 
 Activation : Independent elementwise Sigmoid: 
 \[P_k(y, x) = \sigma(z_k(y, x)) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_k(y, x)}} \in (0, 1)\] 
 
 
 Semantics : Channels do not compete. The probability of Defect A has zero mathematical influence on the probability of Defect C. 
 
 Inference Rule : Per-channel thresholding:  \(\hat{Y}_k(y, x) = \mathbb{I}(P_k(y, x) \ge \tau_k)\) . 
 
 
 Paradigm B: The 5-Channel Multi-Class Softmax Head 
 In this formulation, the model treats every pixel as belonging to exactly one mutually exclusive category. 
 Paradigm B Pipeline:
Decoder Features [B, C, H, W]
  │
  ▼
1×1 Conv Head ──► Raw Logits Z: [B, 5, 128, 800]  (Unbounded in (-∞, +∞))
  │               (Class 0: Background, Classes 1..4: Defects A, B, C, D)
  │
  ├─► Training Flow:   Fed to nn.CrossEntropyLoss() against Integer Target Y: [B, 128, 800] ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
  │
  └─► Inference Flow:  P_k = e^(z_k) / Σ_j e^(z_j) ──► Argmax / Score Filter ──► Categorical Map 
 
 Output Tensor :  \([B, 5, 128, 800]\) . An explicit  Channel 0 represents Background (clean steel) , while Channels 1 through 4 represent defects  \([a, b, c, d]\) . 
 Target Tensor :  \([B, 128, 800]\)  int64 tensor where each pixel contains a single class index:  \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\) . 
 
 Activation : Channel-wise Softmax: 
 \[P_k(y, x) = \frac{e^{z_k(y, x)}}{\sum_{j=0}^{4} e^{z_j(y, x)}}, \quad \text{such that } \sum_{k=0}^{4} P_k(y, x) = 1.0\] 
 
 
 Semantics : Channels compete directly. If logit  \(z_a\)  rises, it directly forces down the probabilities  \(P_{\text{bg}}\)  and  \(P_c\) . 
 
 
 Inference Rule : Pixel-wise argmax or background-gated thresholding: 
 \[\hat{C}(y, x) = \arg\max_{k \in \{0..4\}} P_k(y, x)\] 
 
 
 
 2. The Synthetic Two-Defect Pixel Experiment 
 To see the practical consequence of this choice, let us trace a single fictional pixel  \([y=45, x=320]\)  where the neural network detects strong visual evidence for  both Defect A (a scratch) and Defect C (an inclusion) . 
 Suppose the network's final layer outputs the following raw unbounded logits across all five potential categories: 
 \[z_{\text{bg}} = -1.0, \quad z_a = +2.5, \quad z_b = -4.0, \quad z_c = +2.1, \quad z_d = -3.0\] 
 Case 1: Interpreting Under 4-Channel Multi-Label Sigmoid 
 Under the multi-label paradigm, we ignore  \(z_{\text{bg}}\)  and compute independent probabilities for the four defect classes: 
 \[P_a = \sigma(2.5) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-2.5}} \approx \mathbf{0.9241} \quad (92.4\%)\] 
 \[P_b = \sigma(-4.0) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{4.0}} \approx \mathbf{0.0180} \quad (1.8\%)\] 
 \[P_c = \sigma(2.1) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-2.1}} \approx \mathbf{0.8909} \quad (89.1\%)\] 
 \[P_d = \sigma(-3.0) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{3.0}} \approx \mathbf{0.0474} \quad (4.7\%)\] 
 Mathematical Observations: 
 
 
 Sum of Probabilities : 
 \[\sum_{k=a}^d P_k = 0.9241 + 0.0180 + 0.8909 + 0.0474 = \mathbf{1.8804} \quad (\gg 1.0!)\] 
 Sigmoid probabilities  do not sum to 1.0 . Each channel operates as an independent Bernoulli probability trial. 
 
 
 Decision Outcome :
   If we apply a standard decision threshold  \(\tau = 0.5\) : 
 
 Defect A is  ACTIVE  ( \(0.9241 \ge 0.5\) ). 
 Defect C is  ACTIVE  ( \(0.8909 \ge 0.5\) ). 
 The model predicts that this single pixel simultaneously contains  both a scratch and an inclusion ! 
 
 
 
 
 Case 2: Interpreting Under 5-Channel Multi-Class Softmax 
 Now let us interpret the exact same logits using the categorical Softmax formulation (including  \(z_{\text{bg}} = -1.0\) ): 
 
 
 Compute exponents  \(e^{z_j}\) : 
 \[e^{-1.0} \approx 0.3679, \quad e^{2.5} \approx 12.1825, \quad e^{-4.0} \approx 0.0183, \quad e^{2.1} \approx 8.1662, \quad e^{-3.0} \approx 0.0498\] 
 
 
 Sum of exponents: 
 \[\sum_{j=0}^{4} e^{z_j} = 0.3679 + 12.1825 + 0.0183 + 8.1662 + 0.0498 = \mathbf{20.7847}\] 
 
 
 Compute normalized probabilities  \(P_k = e^{z_k} / \sum e^z\) : 
 \[P_{\text{bg}} = \frac{0.3679}{20.7847} \approx \mathbf{0.0177} \quad (1.8\%)\] 
 \[P_a = \frac{12.1825}{20.7847} \approx \mathbf{0.5861} \quad (58.6\%)\] 
 \[P_b = \frac{0.0183}{20.7847} \approx \mathbf{0.0009} \quad (0.1\%)\] 
 \[P_c = \frac{8.1662}{20.7847} \approx \mathbf{0.3929} \quad (39.3\%)\] 
 \[P_d = \frac{0.0498}{20.7847} \approx \mathbf{0.0024} \quad (0.2\%)\] 
 
 
 Mathematical Observations: 
 
 
 Sum of Probabilities : 
 \[\sum_{k=0}^{4} P_k = 0.0177 + 0.5861 + 0.0009 + 0.3929 + 0.0024 \equiv \mathbf{1.0000} \quad (\text{Exactly } 1.0)\] 
 
 
 The Suppression Effect (Cross-Channel Competition) :
   Notice what happened to Defect C: under Sigmoid, its confidence was  \(89.1\%\) . But under Softmax, because it had to compete against Defect A's slightly stronger logit ( \(2.5 > 2.1\) ), Defect C was  suppressed down to  \(39.3\%\) ! 
 
 
 Decision Outcome :
   If applying argmax: 
 \[\hat{C} = \arg\max \{0.018, 0.586, 0.001, 0.393, 0.002\} = \mathbf{\text{Class 1 (Defect A)}}\] 
 Defect A claims the pixel exclusively. Defect C is completely zeroed out. 
 
 
 
 Why Neither Activation Proves Accuracy or Calibration 
 Students often believe that Softmax probabilities are "more reliable" because they sum to 1.0, or that Sigmoid is "more honest" because channels do not compete. 
 Both beliefs are incorrect : 
 
 Softmax outputs are notoriously  overconfident : even when an input is out-of-distribution or noisy, the exponentiation forces probabilities to sum to 1.0, often assigning  \(99\%\)  probability to an incorrect class simply because one logit happened to be slightly less negative than the others. 
 Sigmoid outputs can be  severely uncalibrated : a model can predict  \(P=0.85\)  on hundreds of false-alarm background speckles if class imbalance is not properly compensated in the loss. 
 Calibration is a property of the model's training dynamics and loss function, not the activation function. 
 
 
 3. Co-occurrence vs. Overlap: The Mask Audit Protocol 
 A dangerous trap in exploratory data analysis is assuming that  image-level co-occurrence implies pixel-level overlap : 
 
 WARNING : Just because an image contains annotations for both  defect_a  and  defect_c  in  train.csv  does  NOT  mean they share a single physical pixel! 
 
 Consider an industrial steel strip: 
 
 A mechanical scratch ( defect_a ) may run along the top edge of the sheet from  \(x=100\)  to  \(x=300\) ,  \(y=10\text{--}15\) . 
 A chemical inclusion cluster ( defect_c ) may sit near the bottom edge from  \(x=600\)  to  \(x=700\) ,  \(y=90\text{--}110\) . 
 Both defects exist on the same strip , but their masks are  \(100\%\)  spatially disjoint  (they share zero pixels). 
 
 
 Figure 4.2: The empirical mask overlap audit flowchart. You must audit your own training dataset to verify whether ground truth masks physically intersect before choosing a target representation. 
 
 How to Audit Your Own Annotations 
 Before choosing between a 4-channel multi-label head and a 5-channel softmax head,  you must execute an empirical pixel-level overlap audit on your dataset . 
 Here is the exact mathematical audit procedure: 
 
 Identify all training images that contain  two or more active defect annotations  ( \(N_{\text{defects}} \ge 2\) ). 
 
 For each multi-defect image, decode the RLE strings into separate binary masks: 
 \[M_a, M_b, M_c, M_d \in \{0, 1\}^{128 \times 800}\] 
 
 
 For every unique pair of classes  \((i, j)\)  where  \(i \ne j\) , compute the  pixel-wise intersection : 
 \[\text{Intersection}(i, j) = \sum_{y=1}^{128} \sum_{x=1}^{800} \left( M_i(y, x) \cdot M_j(y, x) \right)\] 
 
 
 Sum the intersections across your entire training dataset. 
 
 
 # Educational Audit Snippet: How to verify mask overlap yourself
def audit_mask_overlap(dataset):
    total_multi_label_images = 0
    total_overlapping_pixels = 0
    pairwise_overlaps = {}

    for sample in dataset:
        masks = sample["mask"] # Tensor shape: [4, 128, 800]
        active_channels = (masks.sum(dim=(1, 2)) > 0).nonzero().flatten().tolist()

        if len(active_channels) >= 2:
            total_multi_label_images += 1
            # Check pairwise intersection
            for i in range(len(active_channels)):
                for j in range(i + 1, len(active_channels)):
                    c1, c2 = active_channels[i], active_channels[j]
                    intersection = (masks[c1] * masks[c2]).sum().item()
                    pair_key = f"{c1}_vs_{c2}"
                    pairwise_overlaps[pair_key] = pairwise_overlaps.get(pair_key, 0) + intersection
                    total_overlapping_pixels += intersection

    print(f"Audit Summary:")
    print(f"  • Multi-defect images audited: {total_multi_label_images}")
    print(f"  • Total overlapping pixels found: {total_overlapping_pixels}")
    return pairwise_overlaps 
 
 4. The Information Loss Hazard: Forcing Overlaps into Integers 
 What happens if you skip this audit and blindly convert multi-label masks into a single categorical integer target  [B, 128, 800] ? 
 Suppose two defects  genuinely overlap  at pixel  \((y, x)\) , such that: 
 \[M_a(y, x) = 1.0 \quad \text{AND} \quad M_c(y, x) = 1.0\] 
 To feed this into  nn.CrossEntropyLoss() , you must map each pixel to a single integer class index  \(Y \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\) .
If you use  argmax  or priority ordering (e.g., assigning the pixel to Class 1): 
 \[Y(y, x) = 1 \quad (\text{Defect A})\] 
 The Permanent Information Loss: 
 
 Defect C is Completely Erased : The ground truth that Defect C exists at  \((y, x)\)  is permanently deleted from the target tensor. 
 Contradictory Gradient Penalty : When the model forward pass runs, if the network correctly detects visual features of Defect C and outputs a high logit  \(z_c\) ,  CrossEntropyLoss  will  actively penalize the model for being right ! The loss will backpropagate negative gradients into the Defect C channels because the integer target says the pixel is  only  Defect A. 
 Metric Degradation : At evaluation time, your ground truth evaluation mask still contains Defect C. The model, having been trained never to predict Defect C at that location, will suffer false negatives. 
 
 Core Principle : 
 
 If the audit reveals overlapping pixels : You  must  use the 4-channel multi-label Sigmoid formulation to preserve full ground truth fidelity. 
 If the audit reveals zero overlapping pixels : Then the ground truth forms a strict physical partition. In that case, both 4-Sigmoid and 5-Softmax are mathematically valid, and you should compare them empirically on your validation set. 
 
 
 5. The Competing Output Hazard in Independent Heads 
 Suppose your audit shows that ground truth masks are  \(100\%\)  disjoint, and you choose to train with a 4-channel independent Sigmoid head. 
 Are you completely safe?  No! 
 Because the four channels are trained independently,  the model has no architectural constraint preventing it from predicting multiple defects at the same pixel during test inference : 
 
 At training time, the loss separately encourages Channel A and Channel C to match their respective targets. 
 At test time, an ambiguous defect (such as an inclusion surrounded by scratch marks) might produce  \(P_a = 0.72\)  and  \(P_c = 0.68\) . 
 Both probabilities exceed the threshold  \(\tau = 0.5\) . 
 
 The Kaggle Submission & Evaluation Hazard 
 If the competition evaluation metric assumes that masks are mutually exclusive, or if multi-class collisions are heavily penalized by false positive metrics, predicting two overlapping defect masks on the same pixel damages your score. 
 Collision Resolution Strategies for Sigmoid Heads 
 If you use independent sigmoid channels, you must implement an explicit  post-processing collision resolution rule : 
 
 
 Highest Probability Wins (Argmax over Active Channels) :
   If a pixel has  \(P_a \ge \tau\)  and  \(P_c \ge \tau\) , assign the pixel exclusively to whichever class has the higher probability ( \(\max(P_a, P_c)\) ) and zero out the other channel. 
 
 
 Area-Based Precedence :
   Assign the pixel to the defect class with the smaller overall component area (since small rare defects like  defect_b  are more vulnerable to recall penalties). 
 
 
 
 6. Comparative Decision Matrix 
 
 
 
 Dimension 
 4-Channel Multi-Label Sigmoid 
 5-Channel Multi-Class Softmax 
 
 
 
 
 Output Logits 
 \([B, 4, 128, 800]\) 
 \([B, 5, 128, 800]\)  (includes background) 
 
 
 Target Tensor 
 \([B, 4, 128, 800]\)  float32 binary 
 \([B, 128, 800]\)  int64 categorical 
 
 
 Mathematical Assumption 
 Channels are independent. 
 Classes are strictly mutually exclusive. 
 
 
 Ground Truth Overlap Safe? 
 Yes : Preserves overlapping labels losslessly. 
 No : Causes permanent ground truth information loss. 
 
 
 Test-Time Collision Risk 
 Yes : Can predict overlapping masks unless resolved. 
 Zero : Softmax guarantees mutually exclusive output. 
 
 
 Empty Clean Image Handling 
 Implicit: all 4 channels  \(< \tau\) . 
 Explicit: Channel 0 ( \(P_{\text{bg}}\) ) exceeds defect channels. 
 
 
 Loss Compatibility 
 BCEWithLogitsLoss  + Soft Dice. 
 CrossEntropyLoss  + Multiclass Dice. 
 
 
 
 
 7. Common Implementation Pitfalls and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Diagnostic & Fix 
 
 
 
 
 Missing Background Channel in Softmax 
 Outputting 4 channels with  CrossEntropyLoss  without a background class. 
 Network is forced to assign every clean background pixel to one of the 4 defects! Loss explodes. 
 Softmax heads must output  5 channels  ( \(C_0 = \text{background}\) ). 
 
 
 Double Activation Bug 
 Calling  torch.sigmoid(logits)  before passing to  nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() . 
 Loss plateaus near  \(\approx 0.693\) ; gradients vanish. 
 Pass raw unbounded logits directly to  BCEWithLogitsLoss . 
 
 
 Target Type Error in CrossEntropy 
 Passing float targets  [B, 5, H, W]  to  nn.CrossEntropyLoss() . 
 RuntimeError: Expected floating point target with same shape, or int64 target . 
 Pass  [B, H, W]  with  dtype=torch.long  (int64) containing class indices. 
 
 
 Silent Overlap Erasure 
 Converting multi-label masks to integers using  torch.argmax()  without checking for ties or overlaps. 
 Certain defect classes lose up to  \(20\%\)  of their positive training pixels. 
 Run the overlap audit (Section 3) before creating integer targets. 
 
 
 
 
 8. Ungraded Try-It Activity: Trace a Multi-Channel Collision 
 Try this small calculation on paper: 
 Suppose a pixel outputs the following 5 logits: 
 \[z_{\text{bg}} = 0.5, \quad z_a = 1.8, \quad z_b = -2.0, \quad z_c = 1.2, \quad z_d = -1.5\] 
 
 Calculate the Sigmoid probability for Defect A ( \(z_a = 1.8\) ) and Defect C ( \(z_c = 1.2\) ). 
 Using threshold  \(\tau = 0.5\) , which defects are active under the Sigmoid head? 
 Calculate the Softmax probabilities for all 5 classes. Which class wins the argmax? 
 What happened to Defect C's decision between the two heads? 
 
 
 Click here to view the worked solution 
 
 Sigmoid probabilities : 
 \(P_a = \sigma(1.8) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-1.8}} \approx \frac{1}{1 + 0.1653} \approx \mathbf{0.858}\) 
 \(P_c = \sigma(1.2) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-1.2}} \approx \frac{1}{1 + 0.3012} \approx \mathbf{0.768}\) 
 
 
 Sigmoid decision ( \(\tau = 0.5\) ) : 
 Both  \(P_a \ge 0.5\)  and  \(P_c \ge 0.5\) . 
 Both Defect A and Defect C are active! 
 
 
 Softmax probabilities : 
 Exponents:  \(e^{0.5} \approx 1.649\) ,  \(e^{1.8} \approx 6.050\) ,  \(e^{-2.0} \approx 0.135\) ,  \(e^{1.2} \approx 3.320\) ,  \(e^{-1.5} \approx 0.223\) . 
 Sum of exponents:  \(1.649 + 6.050 + 0.135 + 3.320 + 0.223 = \mathbf{11.377}\) . 
 \(P_{\text{bg}} = 1.649 / 11.377 \approx \mathbf{0.145}\) 
 \(P_a = 6.050 / 11.377 \approx \mathbf{0.532}\) 
 \(P_b = 0.135 / 11.377 \approx \mathbf{0.012}\) 
 \(P_c = 3.320 / 11.377 \approx \mathbf{0.292}\) 
 \(P_d = 0.223 / 11.377 \approx \mathbf{0.020}\) 
 Argmax Winner:  Class 1 (Defect A) with  \(53.2\%\) . 
 
 
 Comparison :
   Under Sigmoid, Defect C was confidently predicted as present ( \(76.8\%\) ). Under Softmax, Defect C was suppressed ( \(29.2\%\) ) and completely discarded by argmax!

👉  docs/milestone_3_student_guide/examples/toy_head_comparison.py

 PyTorch Documentation:  torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss . Multi-class categorical cross-entropy and class-weighting mechanics.  PyTorch Docs . 
 Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., & Courville, A. (2016) .  Deep Learning  (Chapter 6: Deep Feedforward Networks). MIT Press. Explains cross-entropy, softmax saturation, and log-likelihood optimization.

title: Guide 05 · BCE, Dice, & Compound Losses
text:
Segmentation Loss Functions: BCE, Dice, & Compound Objectives 
 In standard computer vision tasks, choosing a loss function is straightforward: classification models use Cross-Entropy, while regression models use Mean Squared Error. In industrial anomaly segmentation, however, standard loss functions fail completely because of  extreme spatial class imbalance : 
 
 In our line-scan setting, more than  \(97\%\)  of all pixels across the dataset belong to defect-free background steel . 
 Certain rare anomaly types (such as  defect_b ) occupy less than  \(0.02\%\)  of the total canvas area. 
 
 If you train a neural network using standard, unweighted Binary Cross-Entropy, the model discovers a trivial shortcut:  predict all zeros everywhere . By predicting that every single pixel is clean background, the model achieves over  \(97\%\)  pixel-level accuracy while achieving a  Dice score of exactly 0.0  on defects! 
 To force the network to detect hairline anomalies, you must design a loss function that balances pixel-level classification accuracy against global region overlap. 
 This guide explores  Binary Cross-Entropy with Logits , derives the differentiable  Soft Dice Loss , explains how they respond to missed defects and false alarms on tiny synthetic matrices, analyzes the compound objective  \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}\) , and establishes the critical distinction between your  differentiable training loss  and your  discrete evaluation metric . 
 
 1. The Anatomy of Class Imbalance: Why Pixel Accuracy Misleads 
 Consider a single industrial strip of dimension  \(128 \times 800\) , containing  \(102,400\)  pixels.
Suppose the strip contains a small scratch ( defect_a ) spanning  \(50\)  pixels . 
 Let us examine two hypothetical models: 
 Strip Canvas: 102,400 Pixels | Ground Truth Defect: 50 Pixels (0.049% of Canvas)

Model Alpha (Trivial Background Predictor):
- Predicts 0 on all 102,400 pixels
- Pixel Accuracy: (102,400 - 50) / 102,400 = 99.951%
- Dice Score:     2 * 0 / (0 + 50) = 0.0000 (Completely Useless!)

Model Beta (Real Defect Detector with Slight Jitter):
- Correctly predicts 40 defect pixels, misses 10 defect pixels, predicts 30 false positive pixels
- Pixel Accuracy: (102,320) / 102,400 = 99.922% (Lower accuracy than Model Alpha!)
- Dice Score:     2 * 40 / (70 + 50) = 0.6667 (High Industrial Value!) 
 If your loss function optimizes raw pixel accuracy, the optimizer will actively favor Model Alpha over Model Beta! To train a viable anomaly detector, your objective function must penalize missed foreground pixels much more heavily than background errors. 
 
 2. Binary Cross-Entropy with Logits 
 Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) measures the cross-entropy between independent Bernoulli distributions at each individual pixel. 
 Mathematical Formulation 
 For a ground truth binary target  \(y \in \{0, 1\}\)  and a predicted probability  \(p = \sigma(z) \in (0, 1)\) : 
 \[\ell_{\text{BCE}}(p, y) = - \left[ y \log(p) + (1 - y) \log(1 - p) \right]\] 
 The Numerical Stability of Log-Sum-Exp 
 In naive implementations, students often compute:
 # DANGEROUS: Susceptible to underflow and NaN!
probs = torch.sigmoid(logits)
loss = - (targets * torch.log(probs + 1e-7) + (1 - targets) * torch.log(1 - probs + 1e-7)) 
When a logit is large and negative (e.g.,  \(z = -80\) ),  \(\sigma(z)\)  underflows to  0.0 , causing  \(\log(0.0) = -\infty\)  and yielding  NaN  gradients. 
 PyTorch's  nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()  avoids this by combining the sigmoid and the log-loss into a single mathematically equivalent expression using the  log-sum-exp trick : 
 \[\ell(z, y) = \max(z, 0) - z \cdot y + \log\left( 1 + e^{-|z|} \right)\] 
 This formula is guaranteed to be numerically stable across the entire real number line  \((-\infty, +\infty)\) . 
 Positive Weighting ( pos_weight ) 
 To counteract the overwhelming background majority,  BCEWithLogitsLoss  provides a  pos_weight  parameter ( \(w_{\text{pos}} > 1\) ): 
 \[\ell_{\text{weighted}}(z, y) = - \left[ w_{\text{pos}} \cdot y \log(\sigma(z)) + (1 - y) \log(1 - \sigma(z)) \right]\] 
 Setting  \(w_{\text{pos}} = 10.0\)  scales the loss contribution of positive defect pixels by  \(10\times\) , preventing background pixels from dominating gradient updates. 
 
 3. Soft Dice Loss: Differentiable Overlap Optimization 
 While BCE evaluates each pixel independently in isolation, the  Sørensen–Dice coefficient  (the competition's primary evaluation metric) evaluates the  global volumetric overlap  between the predicted segmentation region  \(\hat{Y}\)  and the ground truth mask  \(Y\) : 
 \[\text{Dice}(\hat{Y}, Y) = \frac{2 |\hat{Y} \cap Y|}{|\hat{Y}| + |Y|} = \frac{2 \sum_i \hat{Y}_i Y_i}{\sum_i \hat{Y}_i + \sum_i Y_i}\] 
 However, the standard Dice coefficient uses discrete binary masks  \(\hat{Y} \in \{0, 1\}\) , which require a threshold step function  \(\mathbb{I}(p \ge 0.5)\) . The step function has a derivative of zero everywhere (and is undefined at the threshold), making it  non-differentiable . 
 The Soft Dice Formulation 
 To make Dice amenable to backpropagation with gradient descent, Milletari et al. (2016) introduced  Soft Dice : replacing discrete binary predictions  \(\hat{Y}_i \in \{0, 1\}\)  with  continuous predicted probabilities  \(P_i = \sigma(z_i) \in [0, 1]\) : 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}(P, Y) = 1 - \frac{2 \sum_{i} P_i Y_i + \epsilon}{\sum_{i} P_i + \sum_{i} Y_i + \epsilon}\] 
 where  \(\epsilon\)  (typically  \(1.0\) ) is a  smoothing constant . 
 Differentiable Soft Dice Flow:
Raw Logit z ──► Sigmoid: P = σ(z) ──► Dot Product with Target: Σ(P * Y) ──► Soft Dice Loss
                                                                            (Fully Differentiable!) 
 The Crucial Role of the Smoothing Factor  \(\epsilon\) 
 The smoothing constant  \(\epsilon\)  serves two essential mathematical purposes: 
 
 Division by Zero Protection : If both the prediction and the ground truth are completely empty ( \(P = \vec{0}, Y = \vec{0}\) ), the fraction resolves to  \(\frac{0 + \epsilon}{0 + \epsilon} = 1.0\) , yielding a loss of  \(1 - 1.0 = \mathbf{0.0}\) . 
 
 Gradient Regularization on Clean Images :
   When an image has  zero defects  ( \(Y_i = 0\)  for all pixels): 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}(P, \vec{0}) = 1 - \frac{\epsilon}{\sum_i P_i + \epsilon} = \frac{\sum_i P_i}{\sum_i P_i + \epsilon}\] 
 Notice that when  \(Y = \vec{0}\) , Soft Dice acts as a smooth, nonlinear  \(L_1\) -like penalty on false positive probabilities ! Any positive probability mass  \(\sum P_i\)  pushes the loss above 0. 
 
 
 
 4. How BCE and Dice Respond to Common Failure Modes 
 To understand why practitioners combine both losses, let us compare how BCE and Soft Dice respond to three realistic defect failure modes on a tiny synthetic canvas of  \(16\)  pixels ( \(4 \times 4\) ). 
 
 Figure 5.1: Comparative behavior of BCE and Soft Dice under three operational scenarios: missed small defects, scattered false alarm noise, and clean empty masks. 
 Case 1: A Missed Small Defect (1 Defect Pixel on 16-Pixel Canvas) 
 
 Ground Truth:  \(1\)  positive pixel,  \(15\)  background pixels. 
 Prediction: The model outputs  \(P = 0.10\)  on the defect pixel (a severe false negative), and  \(P = 0.05\)  on background pixels. 
 
 \[\text{BCE Loss} \approx \frac{1}{16} \left[ - \log(0.10) - 15 \log(0.95) \right] = \frac{1}{16} [2.302 + 0.769] = \mathbf{0.192}\] 
 \[\text{Soft Dice Loss} = 1 - \frac{2(0.10 \times 1) + 1.0}{(0.10 + 15 \times 0.05) + 1.0 + 1.0} = 1 - \frac{1.20}{2.85} = \mathbf{0.579}\] 
 Observation : 
 
 BCE produces a tiny loss value ( \(0.192\) ) because 15 background pixels were predicted reasonably well. 
 Soft Dice produces a massive loss penalty ( \(0.579\) ) because the overlap on the defect was near zero. 
 Takeaway : Soft Dice strongly penalizes missed small defects where BCE remains indifferent. 
 
 
 Case 2: Scattered False Positive Noise (4 TP + 4 FP) 
 
 Ground Truth:  \(4\)  positive pixels. 
 Prediction: Model correctly predicts all  \(4\)  defect pixels with  \(P = 0.95\) , but  also predicts 4 false positive background pixels with  \(P = 0.95\) . 
 
 \[\text{BCE Loss} \approx \frac{1}{16} \left[ 4(-\log(0.95)) + 4(-\log(0.05)) + 8(-\log(0.95)) \right] \approx \mathbf{0.783}\] 
 \[\text{Soft Dice Loss} = 1 - \frac{2(4 \times 0.95) + 1.0}{(8 \times 0.95) + 4.0 + 1.0} = 1 - \frac{8.60}{12.60} = \mathbf{0.317}\] 
 Observation : 
 
 BCE produces a high loss ( \(0.783\) ) because predicting  \(P=0.95\)  on background carries a severe individual cross-entropy penalty ( \(-\log(0.05) \approx 2.99\) ). 
 Soft Dice produces a moderate loss ( \(0.317\) ) because the numerator still captured strong true positive overlap ( \(4 \times 0.95\) ). 
 Takeaway : BCE acts as a strong anchor against scattered false positive speckles. 
 
 
 Case 3: Completely Empty Clean Image ( \(Y = \vec{0}\) ) 
 
 Ground Truth:  \(0\)  defect pixels everywhere. 
 Prediction: Model outputs low background noise ( \(P = 0.12\) ) across the entire  \(16\) -pixel canvas ( \(\sum P_i = 1.92\) ). 
 
 \[\text{BCE Loss} = - \log(1 - 0.12) = - \log(0.88) \approx \mathbf{0.127}\] 
 \[\text{Soft Dice Loss} = \frac{1.92}{1.92 + 1.0} = \mathbf{0.658}\] 
 Observation : 
 
 Soft Dice heavily penalizes accumulated background probability volume on clean sheets, pushing the model toward zero predictions on empty images. 
 
 
 5. The Compound Loss: Combining BCE and Soft Dice 
 Because BCE and Soft Dice possess complementary strengths, standard industry practice combines them into a  compound loss objective : 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} \quad \text{or} \quad \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}\] 
 Complementary Roles in Compound Loss:
BCE Term:       Provides smooth, well-conditioned pixel gradients; anchors background suppression.
Soft Dice Term: Directly optimizes regional overlap; protects rare, small defect boundaries. 
 The Role of the Balancing Coefficient  \(\lambda\) 
 
 If  \(\lambda \ll 1\)  (BCE-dominated): Gradients are smooth and stable, but the model may suffer recall drops on small scratches. 
 If  \(\lambda \gg 1\)  (Dice-dominated): The model focuses heavily on foreground overlap, but training can become volatile, and predictions may develop noisy borders. 
 Do not blindly adopt a fixed  \(\lambda = 1.0\) : You must inspect training logs to ensure neither term overwhelms the other. In standard multi-label setups,  \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}\)  typically starts around  \(0.6\text{--}0.8\) , while  \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}\)  starts around  \(0.9\text{--}1.0\) . 
 
 
 6. Reduction Strategies: Pixel vs. Batch vs. Class 
 How should loss values be averaged across pixels, images, and defect classes? 
 1. Spatial Reduction 
 
 BCEWithLogitsLoss(reduction='mean')  averages across all pixels in the batch ( \(B \times H \times W\) ). 
 
 2. Dice Batch Reduction: Image-Level vs. Global Batch 
 
 
 Image-Level Dice (Default in Segmentation) : Compute Soft Dice separately for each image  \(b \in \{1..B\}\) , then average: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}(P_b, Y_b)\] 
 
 
 Global Batch Dice : Sum intersections and sums across the entire mini-batch before dividing: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} = 1 - \frac{2 \sum_{b, i} P_{b, i} Y_{b, i} + \epsilon}{\sum_{b, i} P_{b, i} + \sum_{b, i} Y_{b, i} + \epsilon}\] 
 Trade-off : Global batch Dice is less volatile on tiny defects, but image-level Dice aligns more closely with per-image competition scoring. 
 
 
 3. Class-Balanced Reduction 
 In multi-label setups, common defects like  defect_c  occur in far more batches than rare defects like  defect_b : 
 
 Unweighted Macro Average : Average across all 4 classes:  \(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{k=1}^4 \mathcal{L}_k\) . 
 
 Class Weighting : Assign explicit weights  \(w_k\)  to underrepresented defect classes: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \sum_{k=a}^d w_k \left( \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}, k} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}, k} \right)\] 
 
 
 
 7. The Critical Boundary: Training Loss vs. Validation Metric 
 One of the most frequent conceptual mistakes in competitive machine learning is conflating the  training loss function  with the  validation evaluation metric . 
 Training Loss (Continuous, Smooth, Differentiable):
Input: Unbounded Logits Z ──► Soft Activations P ──► Continuous Loss Value
Requirement: Must have non-zero, informative gradients everywhere (d L / d z ≠ 0).

Validation Metric (Discrete, Non-Differentiable, Step-Based):
Input: Probabilities P ──► Threshold τ ──► Binary Mask {0, 1} ──► Area Filter ──► Discrete Dice
Requirement: Evaluates the exact operational decision rule of the competition. 
 The Invalidation Trap: Thresholding Inside Training Loss 
 Never threshold probabilities before feeding them into a loss function:
 # FATAL ERROR: Non-differentiable step function breaks backpropagation!
binary_preds = (torch.sigmoid(logits) > 0.5).float()
loss = 1.0 - (2 * (binary_preds * targets).sum() / (binary_preds.sum() + targets.sum()))
loss.backward()  # Gradients are ZERO everywhere! Model will not learn! 
Gradient descent relies entirely on continuous fractional probability adjustments. The loss function must receive soft, differentiable probabilities. 
 
 8. Comparative Decision Matrix 
 
 
 
 Loss Formulation

 Raw Logits  \([B, 4, H, W]\)

 Smooth gradients; excellent background control. 
 Vulnerable to foreground class imbalance.

 Directly optimizes region overlap; immune to pixel imbalance. 
 Noisy gradients on small batches; can drift on empty masks.

 Best of both worlds : balances pixel precision with region overlap. 
 Requires tuning the balancing weight  \(\lambda\) . 
 
 
 Categorical Cross-Entropy

 Enforces strict mutual exclusivity across classes. 
 Requires background class; causes data loss if labels overlap. 
 
 
 
 
 9. Common Implementation Pitfalls and Diagnostics 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Applying Sigmoid before BCEWithLogits 
 Passing probabilities into  nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() . 
 Loss plateaus around  \(\approx 0.693\) ; model fails to converge. 
 Check input range: logits must span  \((-\infty, +\infty)\) , not  \([0, 1]\) . 
 
 
 Omitting Smoothing  \(\epsilon\) 
 Soft Dice denominator has  \(\epsilon = 0\) . 
 Loss explodes to  NaN  on the first clean, defect-free training image. 
 Always set  \(\epsilon \ge 1.0\)  in the Soft Dice formula. 
 
 
 Target Dtype Mismatch in BCE 
 Passing  torch.long  targets to  BCEWithLogitsLoss . 
 RuntimeError: result type Float can't be cast to Long . 
 Ensure targets are  torch.float32 . 
 
 
 Unbalanced Loss Scales 
 BCE is  \(\approx 0.05\)  while Dice is  \(\approx 0.95\) . 
 Gradients from Dice completely overwhelm BCE, causing unstable optimization. 
 Log both loss components separately to W&B; adjust  \(\lambda\)  to balance magnitudes. 
 
 
 
 
 10. Ungraded Try-It Activity: Compute BCE and Soft Dice by Hand 
 Work through this small numerical calculation to verify your understanding: 
 Suppose you have a tiny  \(2 \times 2\)  image patch ( \(4\)  pixels total): 
 
 Ground Truth:  \(Y = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)  (exactly 1 defect pixel at top-left). 
 Predicted Probabilities:  \(P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.1 \end{bmatrix}\) . 
 
 
 Compute the intersection  \(\sum P_i Y_i\) . 
 Compute the sum of predicted probabilities  \(\sum P_i\)  and the ground truth sum  \(\sum Y_i\) . 
 
 Calculate  Soft Dice Loss  with smoothing constant  \(\epsilon = 1.0\) : 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} = 1 - \frac{2 \sum P_i Y_i + 1.0}{\sum P_i + \sum Y_i + 1.0}\] 
 
 
 Compute the pixel-wise BCE loss for the top-left pixel ( \(y=1, p=0.8\) ) and top-right pixel ( \(y=0, p=0.2\) ). 
 
 
 
 Click here to view the worked solution 
 
 
 Intersection : 
 \[\sum P_i Y_i = (0.8 \times 1) + (0.2 \times 0) + (0.1 \times 0) + (0.1 \times 0) = \mathbf{0.80}\] 
 
 
 Cardinalities : 
 \[\sum P_i = 0.8 + 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 = \mathbf{1.20}\] 
 \[\sum Y_i = 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = \mathbf{1.00}\] 
 
 
 Soft Dice Loss : 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} = 1 - \frac{2(0.80) + 1.0}{1.20 + 1.00 + 1.0} = 1 - \frac{1.60 + 1.0}{3.20} = 1 - \frac{2.60}{3.20} = 1 - 0.8125 = \mathbf{0.1875}\] 
 
 
 Pixel-wise BCE : 
 
 Top-left ( \(y=1, p=0.8\) ):  \(-\log(0.8) \approx \mathbf{0.2231}\) 
 Top-right ( \(y=0, p=0.2\) ):  \(-\log(1 - 0.2) = -\log(0.8) \approx \mathbf{0.2231}\) 
 Both pixels contribute equally to the BCE loss!

👉  docs/milestone_3_student_guide/examples/toy_loss_behavior.py

title: Guide 06 · Systematic Model Exploration
text:
Systematic Model Exploration & Controlled Experimentation 
 When transitioning from a simple baseline to advanced deep learning architectures, it is tempting to change multiple components simultaneously: swapping to a larger backbone, modifying the loss function, adjusting learning rates, adding new augmentations, and changing decision thresholds all in a single run. 
 In empirical machine learning, this unstructured approach is known as  "alchemy" . When your validation score changes, you have no scientific way of knowing which component caused the shift: 
 
 Did your score drop because the new backbone was too complex for your dataset, or because your learning rate was too aggressive? 
 Did your score increase because of Soft Dice loss, or because of a lucky random initialization? 
 
 To build a competitive, high-performing segmentation pipeline, you must replace guesswork with  disciplined, controlled experimentation . 
 This guide establishes the  Milestone 3 Controlled Exploration Matrix . You will learn how to design fair single-variable ablations, properly pair output heads with compatible loss functions and target representations, diagnose subtle training failure modes from learning curves, and systematically evaluate your models against holdout validation metrics. 
 
 1. The Golden Rule of Scientific Ablation 
 The foundation of empirical machine learning is the  single-variable ablation principle : 
 
 THE GOLDEN RULE : In every experiment, change exactly  ONE  architectural or hyperparameter choice at a time, while holding all other system variables strictly constant. 
 
 
 Figure 6.1: The Milestone 3 Controlled Exploration Matrix. By holding the split, resolution, optimization schedule, and metric pipeline fixed, each experimental phase cleanly isolates the true causal impact of one design decision. 
 What Must Be Held Constant Across All Experiments? 
 To guarantee fair, unconfounded comparisons: 
 
 Fixed Validation Split : Always evaluate against the exact same combination-stratified holdout fold (e.g., Fold 0 from Milestone 2). Never compare a model trained on Fold 0 against a model trained on Fold 1 or a random split. 
 Fixed Input Resolution & Geometry : Maintain native  \(128 \times 800\)  strip dimensions. Never compare a model trained on cropped  \(128 \times 256\)  patches against one trained on full strips without standardizing evaluation. 
 Fixed Optimization Budget : Keep total epochs (e.g., 30 epochs), optimizer (AdamW), learning rate warmup duration, and effective mini-batch size identical. 
 Fixed Preprocessing & Augmentations : Use the exact same data pipeline (flips, contrast adjustments) across runs. 
 Fixed Evaluation Metric & Post-Processing Grid : Evaluate every candidate using the identical decision pipeline: threshold sweep  \(\tau \in [0.3, 0.8]\)  and minimum connected-component area filtering ( \(A_{\min}\) ). 
 
 
 2. The Milestone 3 Exploration Matrix 
 A rigorous exploration of Milestone 3 unfolds across three structured phases: 
 Exploration Sequence:
Phase 1: Backbone Exploration ──► Phase 2: Grayscale Adaptation ──► Phase 3: Head & Loss Pairing
(Find optimal feature extractor)   (Optimize input mechanics)      (Determine semantic objective) 
 Phase 1: Feature Extractor & Pretraining Ablation 
 Objective : Determine how much benefit transfer learning provides over random initialization, and compare the capacity of ResNet versus EfficientNet backbones. 
 
 Fixed Variables : Grayscale Repeat ( \(3\times\) ), 4-Channel Sigmoid Head, Compound Loss ( \(\text{BCE} + 1.0 \cdot \text{Dice}\) ), 30 Epochs, Fold 0.

 Per-channel threshold  \(\tau_k \in [0.3..0.8]\)  + collision resolution. 
 
 
 Setup Beta (Multi-Class) 
 5 Logits  \([B, 5, 128, 800]\) 
 Integer Class  \([B, 128, 800]\) 
 \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{MultiDice}}\) 
 Pixel-wise Argmax over 5 classes. 
 
 
 
 
 3. Diagnosing Training Dynamics & Failure Modes 
 When training runs complete, do not look solely at the final validation Dice number. Inspect your  learning curves, gradient norms, and per-class metrics  in Weights & Biases to diagnose what the model learned. 
 Common Training Trajectories in W&B:

Trajectory 1 (Healthy Convergence):
Train Loss:  Steady downward slope (0.95 -> 0.35)
Val Dice:    Steady rise (0.10 -> 0.65), plateaus around epoch 20-25

Trajectory 2 (Overfitting):
Train Loss:  Continues dropping to near zero (0.95 -> 0.05)
Val Dice:    Peaks at epoch 12, then steadily degrades (0.60 -> 0.45)
Diagnostic:  Model memorizing training sheet textures; increase weight decay or spatial augmentations.

Trajectory 3 (Class Collapse / Trivial Shortcut):
Train Loss:  Plummets to ~0.03 in epoch 1 and stays flat
Val Dice:    Remains at 0.0000 across all epochs!
Diagnostic:  Model collapsed to all-background prediction; increase Dice weight lambda or pos_weight! 
 Specific Failure Modes in Industrial Strip Segmentation: 
 1. Boundary Erosion 
 
 Symptom : Model detects the general location of defects, but predicted masks are systematically smaller than ground truth (undercounting pixels). 
 Root Cause : Excessive BCE weighting relative to Dice, or threshold  \(\tau\)  set too high (e.g.,  \(0.8\) ). The network avoids false positive penalties by shrinking predicted boundaries. 
 Diagnostic : Plot precision vs. recall. High precision ( \(95\%\) ) paired with low recall ( \(40\%\) ) indicates boundary erosion. 
 
 2. Hairline Scratch Dissolution 
 
 Symptom : Model achieves high Dice on large inclusions ( defect_c ), but achieves near-zero Dice on thin longitudinal scratches ( defect_a ). 
 Root Cause : Receptive field downsampling without adequate skip connection fidelity, or bilinear interpolation smoothing out thin lines. 
 Diagnostic : Inspect per-class Dice scores separately. Never rely on the overall macro average! 
 
 3. False Alarm Speckle Storm 
 
 Symptom : Model predicts dozens of tiny 1-to-3 pixel defect blobs across clean background steel. 
 Root Cause : Dice loss dominates without sufficient BCE anchoring, or threshold  \(\tau\)  set too low ( \(0.2\) ). 
 Diagnostic : Inspect connected-component count per image. Apply minimum area filtering ( \(A_{\min} \ge 50\text{ px}\) ) during post-processing to eliminate isolated sensor noise. 
 
 
 4. Fair Experiment Design: The Controlled Comparison Checklist 
 Before launching an experimental run, verify that your setup satisfies this 6-point checklist: 
 
 [ ]  1. Exact Seed Control : Have you set deterministic random seeds for Python, NumPy, and PyTorch? 
 [ ]  2. Single-Variable Verification : Is exactly  one  component different from your baseline checkpoint? 
 [ ]  3. Data Leakage Isolation : Are training augmentations isolated from the validation set? 
 [ ]  4. Logged Artifacts : Are model checkpoints, hyperparameters, and git commit hashes logged to your experiment tracker? 
 [ ]  5. Compatible Head and Loss : If you changed the output head, did you update both the target tensor format and the loss criterion? 
 [ ]  6. Unbiased Calibration : Are post-processing thresholds evaluated across the  entire validation set , without peeking at the test set? 
 
 
 5. Comprehensive Debugging Matrix 
 
 
 
 Bug / Pitfall 
 Root Cause 
 Observable Symptom 
 Practical Diagnostic 
 
 
 
 
 Exploding Gradients / NaN Loss 
 Pretrained backbone receives large learning rate on epoch 1 without warmup. 
 Loss becomes  NaN  within the first 50 batches; weights become invalid. 
 Clip gradient norms ( nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) ); add linear warmup. 
 
 
 Silent Metric Drift 
 Calculating validation Dice on mini-batches and averaging the ratios instead of accumulating global counts. 
 Validation Dice does not match offline evaluation script. 
 Accumulate True Positives, False Positives, and False Negatives across the full fold before computing Dice. 
 
 
 Dead Defect Channel 
 Rare class ( defect_b ) never receives positive gradient in early epochs. 
 Predicted probabilities for that channel remain  \(< 0.01\)  everywhere. 
 Check positive class count in mini-batches; consider rare-class batch sampling or loss weighting. 
 
 
 Post-Processing Misalignment 
 Post-processing thresholds tuned on training data rather than validation data. 
 Validation score drops significantly relative to training score. 
 Calibrate  \(\tau\)  strictly on held-out validation fold predictions. 
 
 
 
 
 6. Ungraded Try-It Activity: Design an Unbiased Ablation Study 
 Put yourself in the shoes of a lead machine learning engineer: 
 Your pair-programming partner proposes the following experiment to improve your team's baseline: 
 
 "I updated our script! I changed our backbone from ResNet-34 to EfficientNet-B2, increased the learning rate from  \(1 \times 10^{-4}\)  to  \(5 \times 10^{-4}\) , replaced BCE loss with Focal Loss, and evaluated on Fold 2 instead of Fold 0. Our validation score jumped from  \(0.58\)  to  \(0.64\) ! We should adopt all these changes immediately!" 
 
 Questions to answer: 
 
 Identify at least  four confounding variables  in your partner's experiment. 
 Why is the comparison between Fold 0 and Fold 2 invalid? 
 How would you redesign this investigation into a sequence of controlled, single-variable experiments that isolate the true cause of the score improvement? 
 
 
 Click here to view the worked solution 
 
 Four Confounding Variables : 
 Variable 1:  Backbone architecture  (ResNet-34  \(\to\)  EfficientNet-B2). 
 Variable 2:  Learning rate  ( \(1 \times 10^{-4} \to 5 \times 10^{-4}\) ). 
 Variable 3:  Loss function  (BCE  \(\to\)  Focal Loss). 
 Variable 4:  Validation partition  (Fold 0  \(\to\)  Fold 2). 
 
 
 
 Invalidity of Cross-Fold Comparison :
   Different folds contain different subsets of images. Fold 2 might happen to contain easier defect instances or fewer clean images than Fold 0. Comparing scores across different validation splits is scientifically meaningless because the benchmark difficulty changed! 
 
 
 Redesigned Single-Variable Sequence : 
 
 Step 1 (Hold Fold 0, LR  \(1\times 10^{-4}\) , BCE loss constant) : Run ResNet-34 vs. EfficientNet-B2. (Measures backbone impact alone). 
 Step 2 (Take winning backbone from Step 1, hold Fold 0 and BCE loss constant) : Sweep LR  \(1\times 10^{-4}\)  vs.  \(5\times 10^{-4}\) . (Measures optimization impact alone). 
 Step 3 (Take winning backbone and LR from Step 2, hold Fold 0 constant) : Compare BCE vs. Focal Loss. (Measures loss formulation impact alone).
 Now you know exactly which changes helped and which changes hurt! 
 
 
 
 
 
 7. Primary Sources & Further Reading 
 
 Smith, L. N. (2018) .  A disciplined approach to neural network hyper-parameters: Part 1 -- learning rate, batch size, momentum, and weight decay .  arXiv:1803.09820 . Practical methodologies for controlled hyperparameter tuning. 
 Bouthillier, X., et al. (2021) .  Accounting for variance in machine learning benchmarks . MLSys.  arXiv:2103.03082 . Discusses sources of random variation and how to conduct fair empirical comparisons. 
 Weights & Biases Documentation: Best Practices for Hyperparameter Sweeps .  W&B Sweeps Guide . Structuring multi-run experiment grids and tracking metric lineages.

Milestone 3: Synthetic Transfer Learning Walkthrough Notebook 
 This directory contains a self-contained, CPU-runnable educational walkthrough illustrating core concepts from Milestone 3: 
 
 Jupyter Notebook :  synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Paired Python Script :  synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.py 
 
 
 What This Walkthrough Demonstrates 
 
 Synthetic Strip Generation : Synthesizes  \(128 \times 800\)  line-scan steel strips with texture and simulated defect instances (scratch and inclusion) without requiring competition data. 
 Pretrained Backbone Feature Taps : Demonstrates how multi-scale feature hierarchies are tapped from a model across downsampling stages ( \(/2, /4, /8, /16\) ). 
 Grayscale Input Adaptation : Numerically executes and compares three adaptation strategies (3-channel repetition, first conv weight averaging/summing, and a learned  \(1\times 1\)  adapter). 
 Output Head Semantics : Evaluates 4-channel independent sigmoid vs 5-channel mutually exclusive softmax on competing defect logits. 
 Loss Function Comparison : Computes BCEWithLogitsLoss and Soft Dice loss on synthetic masks, showing how each loss responds to missed defects and false alarms. 
 Controlled Training Step : Runs a single forward and backward optimization step on a toy encoder-decoder on CPU in under 2 seconds. 
 
 
 How to Run 
 Option A: Direct Terminal Execution with  uv 
 uv run python docs/milestone_3_student_guide/notebooks/synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.py 
Runs on CPU in ~3 seconds. 
 Option B: Local Jupyter Lab 
 uv run jupyter lab docs/milestone_3_student_guide/notebooks/synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Option C: Google Colab 
 
 Upload  synthetic_transfer_learning_walkthrough.ipynb  to Google Colab. 
 Select a standard CPU runtime (no GPU needed). 
 Execute the cells in sequential order.
